item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship.
Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relentless Milwaukee Brewers team that just kept coming, taking a 6-4 win in Game 4 on Thursday to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champions and advance from the National League Championship Series to their first World Series in 44 years.
After falling behind on Garrett Mitchell’s home run off Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, the Dodgers put the tying run on third base with one out in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings but couldn’t move him another 90 feet. Their dreams of a three-peat were buried under another collection of failed at-bats with a runner in scoring position. They went 2 for 11 in those situations in Game 4 and 5 for 43 in the postseason.
“As a manager and anyone participating in the game, you always wonder … could we have done something different that could have changed the game?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think at the end of the day, we got beat. We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless defensively. They pitched better than we did. They hit better than we did. They slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.
“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no ‘Sorry’s. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”
The New York Yankees of 1998-2000 are still the most recent team to ‘three-peat’ as World Series champions. A National League franchise still hasn’t done it.
“It’s hard to win one. We won two,” Freddie Freeman said. “We went for three and we came up short on a third. Special stuff the past two years. We just came up short this year.”
After losing Game 3 on Wednesday night to become the 42nd team in MLB history to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven series, the Dodgers said all the right things about becoming just the second to climb out of that hole and win the series.
“Four one-game winning streaks,” Dodgers utility player Kiké Hernandez said.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year, ten times, I think,” Manager Dave Roberts said.
Ohtani gave them reason to believe.
With the Brewers rolling out a ‘bullpen game’ in Game 4, opener Shane Drohan was gone after a leadoff single by Kyle Tucker in the second inning. Former Dodger Dustin May replaced him and gave up another single to Teoscar Hernandez, struck out Max Muncy then gave up an RBI single to Andy Pages – the only Dodger who seemed able to hit with a runner in scoring position this postseason.
Kiké Hernandez flew out, bringing Ohtani to the plate with two outs. He struck out against Drohan in the first inning but had finished Game 3 with a 113.5 mph exit velocity on an eighth-inning single – the kind of hard contact missing from Ohtani since mid-August and one of the signs that convinced Roberts to move him back to the leadoff spot for Game 4.
May threw Ohtani a 1-and-1 cutter in at his knees and Ohtani crushed it. It left his bat at 113.1 mph and traveled 428 feet into the right field pavilion. The emotion that burst out of Ohtani was just as explosive. As the crowd roared, he bounced down the first-base line, screaming and gesturing at his teammates in the dugout.
It looked like things were finally turning the Dodgers’ way in this series.
“It’s hard to not say yeah to that,” Muncy said. “He gets that moment, it’s like that’s the swing we’ve been waiting for. We got a nice lead, we got Glas on the mound, we’re confident behind him and they just kept stringing together one good at-bat after another after another after another. They were just kind of relentless.”
The Dodgers’ first home run in the NLCS ended the longest home-run drought of Ohtani’s career at 25 games and 116 plate appearances.
The only thing that seemed longer was how long the Dodgers were going to have to work to make that four-run second inning stand up.
It began disappearing in the fourth inning.
Starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 Brewers in order and struck out six of the first eight. He didn’t have another strikeout. It was nothing but contact from the Brewers after that.
A walk and back-to-back ground-rule doubles – the second by Jake Bauers – cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Glasnow walked the No. 8 hitter, Sal Frelick, who stole second and scored on a single by the No. 9 hitter David Hamilton.
Glasnow was replaced by Evan Phillips who walked three in a row (one intentionally after Hamilton stole second) to force in the tying run.
The four aces the Dodgers thought would give them the upper hand in this postseason did not. Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Glasnow combined for a 6.50 ERA in the series against the Brewers. Only Skubal allowed fewer than three runs in his start.
Tanner Scott came on for the sixth inning. He didn’t give up a home run to a left-handed batter all season. The Brewers’ first batter in the sixth, left-handed Garrett Mitchell, has just two home runs off left-handed pitchers in his 286 career regular-season games.
Scott left a full-count fastball over the heart of the plate and Mitchell, a former UCLA and Orange Lutheran standout, sent it over the center field wall for his second home run off a left-handed pitcher in three at-bats (Blake Snell in Game 3).
The Brewers’ bullpen took over from there. The Dodgers got Kyle Tucker to third base after his one-out double in the sixth, Pages to third after his leadoff double in the seventh and Will Smith to third when Brewers right fielder Frelick fumbled his double in the right field corner.
The six at-bats with a chance to push across the tying run ended in three strikeouts, two ground outs and a shallow pop up to center field.
Hamilton made it a two-run lead with a solo home run in the top of the ninth. It was just the fifth hit of the game for the Brewers.
More to come on this story.

item.title: [mlb.com] Brewers end Dodgers' three-peat bid with an NLCS sweep of their own
item.dc:creator: AJ Cassavell
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- For 363 days, the Brewers dreamed of a different ending. On Thursday night, they wrote it. The script? Familiar enough. A National League Championship Series sweep culminating at Dodger Stadium. Only this time, it was the Brewers who poured from the first-base dugout, celebrating an NL pennant decades in the making -- and celebrating in the very ballpark where their previous season had come to such an unceremonious end. The two-time defending champion Dodgers have been dethroned.
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- For 363 days, the Brewers dreamed of a different ending. On Thursday night, they wrote it.
The script? Familiar enough. A National League Championship Series sweep culminating at Dodger Stadium. Only this time, it was the Brewers who poured from the first-base dugout, celebrating an NL pennant decades in the making -- and celebrating in the very ballpark where their previous season had come to such an unceremonious end.
The two-time defending champion Dodgers have been dethroned. For the first time in 44 years, the Brewers are heading to the World Series. They beat Los Angeles, 6-4, in Game 4 on Thursday night. Next week, Milwaukee will host the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982.
And could this ending have been any more fitting?
Three times in the last decade, the Brewers had been expelled from the postseason by Los Angeles. A year ago, they were swept away with relative ease, as the Dodgers set a course for their second consecutive World Series title. It went unspoken, but all summer, the Brewers seemed to know: If they were going to get where they wanted to go, this was the team they needed to beat.
Thursday’s clincher did not come easy. Why should it? These Brewers don’t do easy. They fell behind 4-0 in the second inning. Dodger Stadium shook when Shohei Ohtani’s titanic three-run blast landed deep in the right-field pavilion.
But the Brewers did what these Brewers do. They answered. Two runs in the fourth. Two more in the fifth. Garrett Mitchell’s go-ahead home run in the sixth, and David Hamilton’s insurance blast in the ninth. Shortly thereafter, the Brewers were celebrating a first in MLB history: They became the first team to sweep the very same team that had eliminated them via sweep in the previous postseason.
Across four games, every punch the Dodgers threw was returned with a Milwaukee counterpunch. Facing elimination on Thursday, Los Angeles moved Ohtani back into the leadoff spot. He’s the best player on the planet, when healthy, and if the Dodgers were going to go down … why go down with anyone else at the top of their lineup?
That meant it was Ohtani who strode to the plate against Brewers right-handed reliever Dustin May with two on and two out in the second. May threw a 1-1 cutter. It hung. Ohtani unleashed that ferocious left-handed swing with a bit of an uppercut. (You know the one, even if it had been a while since you last saw it.) The ball carried to the very back of the right-field pavilion, Ohtani’s first home run since Aug. 18.
Dodger Stadium erupted. The two-time defending champs had life. They led 4-0 in the second inning. They had Tarik Skubal lined up for Game 5. And Yoshinobu Yamamoto for Game 6. And Blake Snell for Game 7. Maybe, just maybe …
The Brewers had other ideas. William Contreras and Jake Bauers hit back-to-back doubles in the fourth, cutting the Dodgers’ lead to 4-2. An inning later, Sal Frelick walked and stole a base, then scored on Hamilton’s RBI single. Tyler Glasnow’s night was done after 4 1/3 innings. A few batters later, Bauers plated the tying run with a bases-loaded walk.
Mitchell led off the sixth by pulverizing a Tanner Scott fastball, and the Brewers had the lead. They held onto it for dear life. Aaron Ashby stranded the tying run in scoring position in the seventh. Then again in the eighth.
He just kept going. Ashby got Kiké Hernández to line out to Jackson Chourio in left field to end it, and with that, the Brewers had their first National League pennant. (When they last reached the Fall Classic in 1982, they did so in the American League.) In the coming weeks, they’ll get a chance for another first: their first World Series title. Either the Rays or Guardians will stand in their way.
But first, a party 44 years in the making.

item.title: [FanSided] Tarik Skubal is more likely to leave the Dodgers after NLCS sweep
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: It felt like the Los Angeles Dodgers were all but guaranteed another World Series title when they acquired Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. Not only did they prevent Skubal from joining a contender like the Brewers, but they added Skubal to a rotation that already included Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Well, the Dodgers were swept in the NLCS by the same Brewers team that they swept just a year ago in the same round, and now, have to look ahead to the offseason. Most of t
item.content:encoded:
It felt like the Los Angeles Dodgers were all but guaranteed another World Series title when they acquired Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. Not only did they prevent Skubal from joining a contender like the Brewers, but they added Skubal to a rotation that already included Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Well, the Dodgers were swept in the NLCS by the same Brewers team that they swept just a year ago in the same round, and now, have to look ahead to the offseason.
Most of their core is locked up (whether that's a good thing or not can be debated), but the one key exception is Skubal, who is slated to hit free agency and search for a record-setting contract. There's a pretty good chance that Skubal is going to surpass Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million deal - the richest for a pitcher in MLB history (excluding Shohei Ohtani, for obvious reasons). Will the Dodgers be the team that pays him, though? It's always possible, but I lean no. Here're a couple of reasons why.
Are we sure the Dodgers will be the high bidder for Tarik Skubal?
This comes down to the money. Tarik Skubal did not hire Scott Boras to represent him to take a hometown discount anywhere. If he did, he'd likely have stayed with the Detroit Tigers. Sure, the Dodgers being perennial contenders in Southern California likely gives them a tiebreaker if all else is equal, but are we sure the Dodgers will be eager to go to insane lengths to keep him around?
Even without Skubal, the Dodgers have a rotation featuring options like Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski, and Roki Sasaki. That is already a group that's as good as any, and as deep as any, without them even making a single addition. Sure, they'd like to have Skubal back, but at what cost?
There will be desperate suitors out there. The New York Mets could use an ace and have Steve Cohen's money to work with, coming off a dismal year. The Toronto Blue Jays are another big-market team in need of pitching with the deep pockets to spend on anybody. The Chicago Cubs might be persuaded to spend on pitching, especially with the Brewers now World Series-bound. Maybe a team like the Philadelphia Phillies will be willing to spend on a super-rotation.
The Dodgers can outbid any of these teams, but will they have the desire to, especially given Mark Walter's recent financial troubles? I'm not sure, especially when considering what they've already invested in their roster.
Dodgers have already invested so much money into their roster
Even the Dodgers have limits. Whether there's a salary cap or not, the Dodgers will only do so much. Given the money they've tied up, are they really willing to spend $300 million or $400 million on Skubal?
| Player | Contract | Age | Final Contract Year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | 10 years, $700 million (with $680 million deferred) | 32 | 2033 |
| Mookie Betts | 12 years, $365 million | 34 | 2032 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 12 years, $325 million | 28 | 2035 (opt-outs after '30, '32) |
| Kyle Tucker | 4 years, $240 million | 29 | 2029 (opt-outs after '27, '28) |
| Blake Snell | 5 years, $182 million | 33 | 2030 (club option) |
| Freddie Freeman | 6 years, $162 million | 37 | 2027 |
| Will Smith | 10 years, $140 million | 31 | 2033 |
| Tyler Glasnow | 5 years, $136 million | 33 | 2028 (club option) |
| Tommy Edman | 5 years, $74 million | 31 | 2030 (club option) |
| Tanner Scott | 4 years, $72 million | 32 | 2028 |
| Edwin Diaz | 3 years, $69 million | 32 | 2029 |
| Teoscar Hernandez | 3 years, $66 million | 34 | 2028 (club option) |
The 2027 season hasn't even begun, yet the Dodgers already have a $393 million luxury tax payroll per Spotrac, the largest in the sport by nearly $50 million. Are they really going to be open to add more than $30 million annually to that, knowing they have other needs to address? I mean, their bullpen was shaky much of the year, and their lineup, clearly, has holes.
Again, even the Dodgers have limits. There's only a certain amount of money they'll be willing to invest. Adding another massive contract to this list feels like a lot to ask for, even for the Dodgers.
The last thing the Dodgers need is another bad contract on their hands
The Dodgers got the most out of the massive contracts they dolled out. Guys like Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Will Smith and Teoscar Hernandez played a major role in their back-to-back World Series wins. It's also worth noting that this foursome had the worst years of their careers and that they're all on the wrong side of 30. Father Time is undefeated, and while the beginnings of these massive contracts are always fun, the later years almost never are.
It's clear that guys like Betts and Freeman are well beyond their respective primes at this point, and while Freeman's contract is expiring after 2027, Betts is locked in for another six years. Smith is under contract for another seven years. Blake Snell can't stay healthy and he's locked in for at least three more years. Based on how he played this year, the Dodgers might be stuck handing Kyle Tucker $60 million annually for the next three years. Ohtani and Yamamoto are players who are still great when healthy, but eventually they'll age. There are bad contracts and the potential for bad contracts everywhere you turn on this Dodgers roster.
Again, giving these deals proved to be worthwhile, with the Dodgers earning back-to-back World Series wins, but there's a clear downside to handing out these insane long-term deals. Are the Dodgers willing to take on the risk with Skubal, who, by the way, had an elbow injury this season and has a pretty scary history of arm injuries?
The overarching takeaway from this series, beyond how good the Brewers looked, is how lethargic the Dodgers looked. They appeared completely overmatched at the plate, and that doesn't feel accidental given how old this roster is. Re-signing Skubal will be great for the short term but will almost certainly not age well. Given all the other bad deals on their roster, adding another one just doesn't feel like the smartest move, and Andrew Friedman is one of the smartest minds in the sport.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers’ manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Thursday that he’s very unlikely to use Tarik Skubal or Yoshinobu Yamamoto out of the bullpen in Game 4 of the NLCS against the Brewers.

Even with their backs against the wall, Roberts maintained confidence when asked if his star hurlers would be available out of the bullpen on Thursday, saying, “No. ... Our bullpen is rested, very, very capable. You’ve still got to win four, but obviously you’ve got to win one first, and I completely understand that. But the short answer, no.” It’s possible that the calculus could change if the Dodgers get down early in Game 4, but for now he appears to have full faith in Tyler Glasnow and his rested bullpen.

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Everything Brewers fans need to know about Dodgers’ Game 4 starter Tyler Glasnow
item.dc:creator: Brandon Glick
item.description: It's sort of a sick joke that, even down 3-0 and having used up their trio of all-universe aces, the Los Angeles Dodgers can trot another frontline starter out to the mound to try and stave off elimination against the Milwaukee Brewers. Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS. Of course, after seeing Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Blake Snell -- who have four Cy Youngs and a World S
item.content:encoded:
It's sort of a sick joke that, even down 3-0 and having used up their trio of all-universe aces, the Los Angeles Dodgers can trot another frontline starter out to the mound to try and stave off elimination against the Milwaukee Brewers. Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS.
Of course, after seeing Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Blake Snell -- who have four Cy Youngs and a World Series MVP between them -- there's not much that should faze the Brewers. Glasnow is a very good pitcher, but he's the closest thing to a weak link in the Dodgers' super-rotation.
Still, he's an intimidating presence on the bump and has had tons of success against most of Pat Murphy's lineup to boot. Milwaukee will counter with rookie southpaw Shane Drohan, though this will be an all-hands-on-deck effort as the Brewers try to get to where they haven't been since 1982.
To sweep Dodgers, Brewers will need to overcome intimidating history against Tyler Glasnow
Let's start with the optimistic view. Glasnow remains a perpetually injury-prone pitcher, making just 13 starts this year while dealing with back spasms and various setbacks. Though that means his arm should be fresh, he also likely isn't operating at 100%; his last start (against the Braves in the NLDS) saw him yield only one hit across 4⅔ innings, but he also walked five batters as part of a laborious outing.
That's an exploitable weakness the Crew need to take advantage of, since Glasnow has walked multiple batters in each of his past five starts. Running up his pitch count early will force Dave Roberts to dig into his stash of relievers, many of whom seemingly don't have his trust right now.
The major concern for the Brewers lies in the past, since Glasnow has had their number historically. Christian Yelich (one hit, seven strikeouts in 14 plate appearances), William Contreras (zero hits in 10 PAs), and Jackson Chourio (.286 OPS in seven PAs) have all struggled mightily in their head-to-head matchups with the right-hander.
Those numbers also don't include his dominant performance in Game 3 of last year's NLCS, when he struck out eight and held the Brewers to one run on three hits over 5⅔ innings. As such, the work of Game 3 hero Jake Bauers (.952 OPS in seven PAs) and Brice Turang (.375 OBP in eight PAs) will be key to getting the Crew ahead tonight.
Having already taken down all of the Dodgers' best arms, the Brewers should enter this one with immense confidence. With a trip to the World Series on the line, all they need to do is crush their Tyler Glasnow demons.

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] Brewers' best (and only) chance for historic playoff redemption in NLCS is in Shane Drohan's hands
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: Much of the media's attention heading into this year's NLCS rematch between the Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers was on the strength of the defending World Series Champions' starting pitching group. With a pair of Cy Young-winning left-handers in Tarik Skubal, whom the Dodgers acquired at the midseason trade deadline, and Blake Snell, as well as 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow in their rotation, that attention was well-deserved. However,
item.content:encoded:
Much of the media's attention heading into this year's NLCS rematch between the Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers was on the strength of the defending World Series Champions' starting pitching group. With a pair of Cy Young-winning left-handers in Tarik Skubal, whom the Dodgers acquired at the midseason trade deadline, and Blake Snell, as well as 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow in their rotation, that attention was well-deserved.
However, through the first three games of the NLCS, the Brewers have bested Los Angeles' top three starters and built a commanding 3-0 series lead. Skubal and Snell took the loss in Games 1 and 3, respectively, and sandwiched in between was a 2.2-inning, 75-pitch start from Yamamoto that forced Dave Roberts to use seven relief pitchers in Game 2. On the other side, Milwaukee's starting group hasn't necessarily been the strength of their pitching staff during the postseason -- that would be their bullpen -- but the trio of Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson, and Robert Gasser combined for 13.1 innings and allowed just two earned runs through the first three NLCS games.
Game 4 is where things get interesting. While the Brewers' decision to start Miz, Henderson, and Gasser in the first three games of the NLCS felt like an obvious one, especially after Gasser's strong showing in the NLDS, who would get the ball to start Game 4 remained an unanswered question through this morning.
However, just moments ago, the Brewers officially revealed that rookie southpaw Shane Drohan will start Game 4 of the NLCS tonight. Drohan, who will be making his postseason debut, will be the first out-getter of Milwaukee's quest for never-before-seen level of redemption in a playoff series.
Brewers trying to become first team in MLB history to sweep a team in the playoffs who swept them in the previous postseason
The Brewers just have to win one of their next four games to return to the World Series for the first time since 1982. That much is true. That said, closing out the Dodgers tonight and completing one of the most impressive sweeps in postseason history would be a redemption performance never before seen in MLB history. According to MLB.com's statistician Sarah Langs, no team in the history of MLB has swept a team in a postseason series after being swept by that same team in the previous playoffs.
After the demoralizing loss that the Brewers suffered in last year's NLCS, defeating the Dodgers in four games this year would easily be one of the most satisfying postseason series sweeps in MLB history. Pair that with the payroll disparity that exists between the two clubs, the fact that Los Angeles is pursuing a three-peat, and the Dodgers' victory in the Tarik Skubal trade deadline sweepstakes, and the Brewers sweeping MLB's Evil Empire would be especially gratifying.
Completing that sweep in Game 4 tonight starts with a strong showing from Drohan, who hasn't pitched in any of the Brewers' first seven postseason games this year. Drohan impressed during the regular season, with a 4.19 ERA in 124.2 innings to prove it. His low arm-slot from the left side matches up well with Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, and his six-pitch mix should keep the struggling Dodgers' offense off-balance.
It likely won't be a long start for Drohan, especially given the arms available in Pat Murphy's 'pen. In theory, only DL Hall is unavailable for tonight's game, but the Brewers may elect to avoid using Abner Uribe for an eighth consecutive game as well. However, that leaves Kyle Harrison, Dustin May, Chad Patrick, Aaron Ashby, Antonio Senzatela, JoJo Romero, and Trevor Megill available for Murphy to turn to after Drohan.
Any type of victory over the Dodgers in this year's NLCS would represent redemption for the Brewers after being swept by Los Angeles a season ago. However, Milwaukee's only shot at historic redemption that has never occurred in the history of MLB is tonight, during which rookie southpaw Shane Drohan will kick off their sweep attempt.

item.title: [si.com] Brewers Are Using Postseason Stage to Showcase MLB’s New Era
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci
item.description: Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out. The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out.
The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell on the mound with a lead and lost all three. Ninety-five million dollars, four Cy Young awards and a World Series MVP worth of pitching and they could not hold back Milwaukee any more than you can hold back water with your hands.
But the most obvious reason why the Brewers have put the Dodger dynasty on the brink of extinction is this: the youngest pitching staff in baseball—and the hardest throwing staff in postseason history—has smothered the oldest team in baseball. Milwaukee is pushing around the aging Dodgers lineup with a barrage of fastballs in three versions, especially power sinkers. They are shoving 66.8% fastballs at the Dodgers at an average velocity of 97.9 mph. The Dodgers’ only path to victory is to slug and the Brewers simply won’t allow it.
“I just think they’re really good pitchers,” Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard, and they’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too much of an opportunity to kind of build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They throw their stuff in the zone—and with all three fastballs. A lot of guys have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball. It’s really hard to put barrels on the ball.
“At the end of the day, it’s just the velocity of their stuff. They throw the ball really hard. And we all know when you throw that hard, it’s really hard.”
The Brewers knew coming into the series that in today’s game older players don’t hit elite fastballs as well as younger players, and so the matchup was to their liking. But this? Who could have seen this in the NLCS? The Dodgers:
- Have two extra-base hits in 105 plate appearances
- Have been outhomered, 5-0
- Are the first team in franchise history to lose three straight games in one postseason with no home runs and no attempted stolen bases
- Are hitting .228 against fastballs
- Are 2-for-16 with runners in scoring position, part of a 3-for-32 postseason disaster in those spots
This has been the year in which baseball made a sharp turn when it comes to the speed of the game. Younger players thrive. Velocity, and the widespread adoption of the family of three fastballs, changed everything. You need fast-twitch athleticism, youthfulness. You need this generation of players who know velocity as a first language. You need rangy players on defense. The numbers bear out that younger players are the preferred way to go.
Players 30 and younger this year hit .247. Players in the 31-35 year-old demographic hit 10 points worse, .237, their worst showing ever. There was a time when front offices valued those 31-35 players because it seemed to be the peak intersection of experience and physical tools. Front offices were afraid to commit to younger players because of the lack of reps and track records. Those days are over.
The difference on the field in NLCS Game 3 was striking. The Brewers are the fastest team in baseball, as measured by sprint speed. The Dodgers are 24th.
The Brewers started a lineup and a pitcher with an average age of 26.1. They became the first team in history with a second postseason game starting three players 22 and younger: leftfielder Jackson Chourio, shortstop Cooper Pratt and rightfielder Luis Lara. Chourio opened the game with a first-pitch homer. Pratt smacked three hits, stole a base and scored a run. Lara flew around rightfield like a bird of prey, snaring anything that dared enter his airspace.
Watching Chourio, 22, Garrett Mitchell, 28, and Lara, 21, patrol the outfield was like watching an Olympic sprint relay team.
On the other side of the field, the Dodgers, especially their bats, looked old and slow. The average age of their starting 10 was 32.3 years old—more than six years older than Milwaukee’s fearless group. Only two starting Dodgers were in their 20s: centerfielder Andy Pages, 25, and Kyle Tucker, 29, who with his diminished range and baserunning has been trending older than his age.
By starting eight players 31 and older, these Dodgers joined the 2023 Dodgers, who got bounced by the Diamondbacks, as the only teams in the past 19 postseasons to trot out so many starting players that old in a game.
Fittingly, the old team played an outdated style of baseball, one from a generation ago. The ninth-place hitter, Tommy Edman, twice batted after the leadoff runner reached first base. Twice manager Dave Roberts did not ask him to bunt.
“I thought about it, but it’s just, he had a good pitch to hit. Flew out,” Roberts said. “I just didn’t feel giving up an out right there. Early in the game, I wanted Tommy to hit ...
“We haven’t been getting hits with runners in scoring position. To give up an out, to bank on getting a hit with runners in scoring position, I’d rather just try to maybe slug, hit a double.”
Edman was a below average hitter (97 OPS+) with a .385 slug this season.
Roberts and the Dodgers keep waiting for slug to show up at the expense of forfeiting the situational baseball as deployed by the other three remaining teams, the youthful Brewers, Guardians and Rays. The Dodgers still may be waiting Thanksgiving morning.
For instance, the Dodgers were down 1-0 in the sixth when Roberts sent 36-year-old Max Muncy to hit for Pages with runners on first and second and no outs. In that situation, the Brewers are bunting. Milwaukee plays get-em-over, get-em-in ball. The Dodgers? No way. Muncy is a three-true outcome guy. He is not going to bunt. Again, the Dodgers played for slug and got nothing. Muncy struck out. Will Smith, 31, did save the rally with a two-run double. But the Dodgers would go 1-for-12 after that against hard-throwing relievers D.L. Hall and Trevor Megill.
The lineup remained cold. Shohei Ohtani, 32, cannot pull a baseball because of lower-half injuries that won’t allow him to properly turn his hips and get to a firm front side. Freeman, 37, has three extra-base hits since Aug. 31.
“[Our] pitching staff has been great, to be honest,” Rojas said. “It’s really hard to put it into context when you have to pitch and have to play defense with a one run lead every single time. It’s like asking these guys to just throw a perfect inning every single time. It’s not sustainable. So, the blame is on the offense. We all know we could’ve done better, but nothing we can do now.”
How in the world has Milwaukee made Los Angeles look so bad?
“It’s pretty simple,” Muncy said. “We’ve played like [poop]. They’ve played great.”
Occam’s razor (or commode) aside, the one-sided NLCS is bigger than that. It stands as a changing of the guard, recalling the 1964 World Series, when the St. Louis Cardinals, emblematic of the National League embracing Black and Latin American players, ended the dynasty of an aging New York Yankees team, then the second oldest team in baseball. The younger, faster, harder-throwing, more creative team has been, beyond doubt, the better team.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [tsn.ca] Bauers’ relentless at-bat have Brewers on brink of World Series after contemplating retirement
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jake Bauers’ new lease on life allows him to worry less and give more.
Two seasons after he nearly quit baseball, Bauers has become a big hitter in the middle of the Milwaukee Brewers’ lineup — and he put his renewed focus on display in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series.
Bauers’ two-run homer on the 11th pitch of a seventh-inning at-bat against Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell gave Milwaukee the lead for good in a 6-2 victory Wednesday, putting the Brewers on the cusp of their first World Series since 1982.
“Incredible at-bat,” manager Pat Murphy said.
Bauers fouled off five two-strike pitches before turning on a 97 mph fastball and launching it 412 feet to right field.
“Super sick,” teammate Garrett Mitchell said. “I think that more just goes to show the type of player he is. It’s a selfless at-bat. He’s just trying to put the ball in play. He’s trying to move the guy over, and put an incredible swing on that. For me, being able to watch that on deck was awesome.”
Mitchell followed with a home run of his own to chase Snell and make it 4-2. Milwaukee has a 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven NLCS, with Game 4 at Los Angeles on Thursday.
Bauers was drafted in 2013 by the San Diego Padres out of Marina High School in Huntington Beach, located about 40 miles south of Dodger Stadium. After batting .202 for the New York Yankees in 2023, he was traded that November to Milwaukee — where he hit .199 in 2024.
Ready to hang up his spikes, Bauer changed his mind when his wife told him she was pregnant. Wanting to be a provider for his growing family, he put off retirement and maintained their health insurance.
Earlier this week, Bauers spoke eloquently about his wife and her sacrifice while raising two rambunctious children while he is away playing baseball.
Now, he’s making fans all over Milwaukee feel like little kids again.
“There’s a lot of people to credit, man,” Bauers said after Wednesday’s game. “I’ve played a lot of places. I’ve picked up knowledge from a lot of different people.
“I think what changed for me this year was I stopped caring about results. I started caring about competing. I started caring about being in the moment and getting out of my own way.”
All that showed up in Game 2 of the series when he worked a two-out walk to load the bases on the 12th pitch he saw from Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto in the third inning. Christian Yelich followed with a two-run single for a 3-2 lead in a 7-4 victory, ending Yamamoto’s outing.
Bauers, who turned 31 last week, is in his third year with Milwaukee — his fifth team in seven major league seasons. The first baseman and corner outfielder led the Brewers with 26 home runs and an .874 OPS during the regular season.
“Jake got an opportunity, that’s what he got,” Murphy said. “He got an opportunity to contribute, and he kind of found his offensive approach. And he kind of found, like, I’m really talented, but this is what serves me best. It’s a growth in the game. He’s continued to grow.”
Patient and disciplined with a sharp eye at the plate, Bauers drew 94 walks and compiled a .389 on-base percentage this season. He also had 86 RBIs in 144 games, shattering his previous career highs across the board.
“I came into this year feeling like there was really only one person holding me back, and that was myself,” Bauers said. “So I think I just gave myself the space to believe that I could play — I could play in this league.”
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
Doug Padilla, The Associated Press

item.title: [Heavy.com] What Dodgers' Dave Roberts Said About Being Down 3-0 in NLCS

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are on the brink of elimination. With a 6-2 loss in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, they are at risk of being swept by the Milwaukee Brewers and watching their chances of a three-peat be dashed.
Manager Dave Roberts has been in this position before as a player. In 2004, the Boston Red Sox faced a 3-0 deficit in the American League Championship Series before rallying to win four games in a row and knock out the New York Yankees before sweeping the St. Louis Cardinals in the World Series. A key stolen base by Roberts in the ninth inning of Game 4 sparked the comeback.
However, after Game 3 of the NLCS, Roberts was asked about the 2004 comeback and made clear that that is not his focus heading into Game 4 against the Brewers.
“They’ve all seen the documentary, so they know it can happen,” Roberts said.
Dave Roberts Weighs in on 2004 ALCS Comeback
It has been 22 years since the Red Sox pulled off their comeback against the Yankees. They were three outs away from being swept out of the playoffs by the Yankees.
Roberts obviously played a key role in that as a player with his stolen base. But the point he makes is that what happened in 2004 is irrelevant. The Dodgers are in the exact same spot as the Red Sox were, but to win this series, the focus isn’t going to be on the past, but rather, what they can do to chip away at the Brewers.
No two situations are going to play out exactly the same, even though the Dodgers are in the same position the Red Sox were all those years ago, this potential comeback will look a lot different.
Things are not looking good for the Dodgers, but Roberts made clear that he doesn’t want his team to dwell on the past and try to find inspiration in something that took place 22 years ago.
What that series proved is that it’s always possible for the unexpected to happen, and it is a reminder that it’s never over until it’s over. But that was a long time ago. The Dodgers have business to take care of and cannot afford to get lost in the past and try to replicate what was done.
They’re going to have to do it their own way. They have won back-to-back World Series titles after all, so there is certainly still some hope.
What’s Next for Los Angeles Dodgers After Game 3 Loss?
The Dodgers have already announced Tyler Glasnow as their Game 4 starter. If they win Game 4, they’ll get the ball back in Tarik Skubal’s hands for Game 5. Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell would be next in line for Games 6 and 7 if the series gets that far. One win could potentially give the Dodgers a little bit of momentum as they try to get back to the World Series and stave off elimination, but there is a lot of momentum that they are already up against as they head into Game 4.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has ruled out using Tarik Skubal or Yoshinobu Yamamoto in relief for Thursday's must-win Game 4 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
According to Ben Nicholson-Smith of Sportsnet, Roberts was asked whether either starter could be available out of the bullpen with the Dodgers facing elimination. His answer was no, leaving Los Angeles to pursue a comeback without either pitcher as a relief option.
The decision comes after Milwaukee defeated Los Angeles 6-2 in Game 3 on Wednesday, pushing the Dodgers into a 3-0 series deficit. The Brewers are now one win away from reaching the World Series for the first time since 1982.
Skubal started Game 1 of the series and allowed two runs over five innings, recording seven strikeouts and two walks. The Dodgers lost that game 2-1, putting the pressure on their rotation early in the series.
Yamamoto started Game 2 but struggled to work deep into the contest. He allowed three runs on four hits and two walks over 2 2/3 innings as Milwaukee secured a 7-4 victory. The right-hander had been named the 2025 World Series MVP after helping Los Angeles win the championship.
The Dodgers entered the postseason after finishing the regular season 100-62, while Milwaukee went 103-59 to earn the National League's top seed. The Brewers have carried that form into the NLCS, winning the first three games and limiting Los Angeles' margin for error.
Tyler Glasnow is scheduled to start Game 4 for the Dodgers. He pitched 4 2/3 innings of one-run baseball in the NLDS-clinching win over the Atlanta Braves, although he issued five walks in that appearance.
The Dodgers must win four consecutive games to advance, beginning Thursday at Dodger Stadium. Only the 2004 Boston Red Sox have overcome a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven MLB postseason series.
Roberts' decision means Los Angeles will need Glasnow and its available bullpen arms to handle the elimination game. Milwaukee, meanwhile, can clinch the NLCS and secure its first World Series berth since 1982 with another victory.
This story was originally published by Athlon on Oct 15, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add Athlon as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.content:encoded:
These Los Angeles Dodgers broke a 25-year streak by becoming the first back-to-back champions with the World Series victory over the Toronto Blue Jays last year.
Since then, all the talk about from the national media has been whether or not they could follow that 1998-2000 New York Yankees squad into the hallowed halls of three-peaters.
Down 2-0 to the Brewers in the NLCS, however, the goal of Game 3 was merely about survival. Which is why Miguel Rojas' cleats suggesting that a third title is on the horizon has naturally garnered quite a lot of attention on social media.
Now faced with the prospect of having to win four games in a row to even advance to the World Series, baseball fans may be waiting for that three-peat to load for quite a long time.
Dodgers have been humbled by Brewers, but they're equipped to make an improbable NLCS comeback
Because the Dodgers have been so dominant for so long, fans of other teams rarely miss their chance dunk on Los Angeles when the opportunity presents itself.
The good news for the Dodgers is that this series isn't over. A 3-0 deficit is daunting, but they're better equipped than most to come back from it. Tyler Glasnow will take the ball tonight against old friend Dustin May, giving Dave Roberts a clear advantage on the mound from the get-go.
If the Dodgers able to stave off the sweep at Chavez Ravine, they'll get one more game at home, this time with Tarik Skubal on the mound. Then, Game 6 in Milwaukee would allow them to deploy Yoshinobu Yamamoto again. After that would come a do-or-die Game 7 with Blake Snell eyeing a chance at redemption after Jake Bauers got the better of him last night.
That's a lot of looking ahead for a team that hasn't won a game in the NLCS to date, but it's a reminder of how stacked this roster is. Even with Jacob Misiorowski waiting in the wings, you'd have to like the Dodgers' chances of winning with Skubal and Yamamoto on the mound if they can get to their next starts.
It all starts with getting back in win column tonight and delaying the inevitable for another day. Failing that, Rojas may need to find the nearest dumpster in which to deposit his custom cleats.

item.content:encoded:
By BETH HARRIS AP Sports Writer
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Milwaukee Brewers hit the second-fewest home runs in baseball during the regular season, even as they topped the majors with 103 wins.
Maybe they were saving their biggest swings for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell launched back-to-back homers off Blake Snell in the seventh inning, and the Brewers beat the Dodgers 6-2 on Wednesday to build a 3-0 cushion in the National League Championship Series.
Jackson Chourio also went deep on the first pitch of the game to help the Brewers close within one win of their first NL pennant. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise reached its only World Series, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals in 1982.
“Job’s not finished yet,” Mitchell said.
Game 4 is Thursday at Dodger Stadium, where the Brewers can become the first major league club to complete a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
Los Angeles took all four games against Milwaukee in the NLCS last year.
The Dodgers had just gone ahead 2-1 in the sixth inning before getting stunned by the Brewers in their three-run seventh. The loss pushed the two-time defending World Series champions to the brink of elimination.
“All three games we’ve played so far, and hopefully that continues, where just every time they score, we come back and score,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. “That’s not easy to do in baseball.”
It was the fifth comeback victory in seven postseason games for the Brewers, who have never beaten Los Angeles in three previous playoff series.
The only other time the Dodgers trailed 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series, they were swept by the Baltimore Orioles in the 1966 World Series.
The lone team in big league history to come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven postseason series was the Boston Red Sox in the 2004 AL Championship Series against the New York Yankees.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “We’ve got to win tomorrow. That’s our only focus.”
Coming into the seventh, Snell had retired 14 batters in a row. But the first pitch of the game thrown by the two-time Cy Young Award winner was hit for a home run by Chourio, and his last pitch was Mitchell’s solo shot.
Andrew Vaughn drew a seven-pitch walk to open the seventh and was replaced by pinch-runner Christian Yelich. Bauers followed with a 412-foot drive to right field on the 11th pitch of his at-bat for a 3-2 lead as most of the players in Milwaukee’s dugout came onto the field to celebrate.
“I was looking for a fastball, and I didn’t want to miss it,” said Bauers, who had a team-leading 26 of Milwaukee’s 154 regular-season homers.
It was his latest relentless plate appearance, too, after Bauers drew a 12-pitch walk from Yoshinobu Yamamoto that helped the Brewers go ahead early in Game 2.
“I think what changed for me this year was I stopped caring about results,” Bauers said. “I started caring about competing. I started caring about being in the moment and getting out of my own way.”
Watching Bauers work over Snell was “super sick,” Mitchell said.
And then it was his turn.
Mitchell’s drive traveled 428 feet to right-center. That chased Snell, who hadn’t given up a home run in 46 1/3 innings this year entering the game. It was the first time in his career he served up back-to-back homers to left-handed hitters and only the second time he gave up multiple longballs to left-handed batters in one game.
Bauers and Mitchell became just the third pair of left-handed hitters with consecutive postseason home runs off the same left-handed pitcher. Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper did it for Philadelphia against Atlanta reliever Dylan Lee in an NL Wild Card Series this year, and Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig connected for the New York Yankees off Bill Sherdel of the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1928 World Series.
Milwaukee has five homers in the NLCS and eight this postseason.
Snell gave up four runs and four hits in six-plus innings. He struck out nine and walked two.
The Brewers extended their lead to 5-2 in the eighth on Justin Wrobleski’s wild pitch that scored Brice Turang, who reached on an infield single and advanced to third on William Contreras’ single. They added another run on Joey Ortiz’s two-strike RBI single in the ninth.
The offensively starved Dodgers took a 2-1 lead on Will Smith’s two-run double off reliever Abner Uribe in the sixth.
After rookie starter Robert Gasser pitched five shutout innings, Uribe entered and loaded the bases on walks to Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker and Shohei Ohtani. Smith, who was 1 for 25 in the playoffs, doubled off the left-center fence with one out for his first hit of the NLCS.
DL Hall took over from Uribe and stranded runners at second and third by striking out pinch-hitter Kiké Hernández and Tommy Edman.
Hall allowed one hit in 2 1/3 scoreless innings to improve to 3-0 in these playoffs. Trevor Megill got four outs for his second save of the series and fourth this postseason.
The Dodgers played from behind again after the 22-year-old Chourio connected for his third career leadoff homer in the postseason as fans were still heading to their seats.
After that, Mitchell walked and Cooper Pratt singled in the second before Snell retired 14 in a row — six on strikeouts — before getting hammered in the seventh.
The Dodgers had runners on base in all but three innings, but couldn’t get enough across. They have yet to homer in the NLCS and are 3 for 32 with runners in scoring position this postseason.
Ohtani was 1 for 2 with a walk while hitting sixth in the order, the lowest he’s batted since joining the Dodgers three years ago.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here

item.title: [amNewYork] Mets rumors: Is Tarik Skubal a legitimate target? | amNewYork

Zac Thornton spoke with Mike Puma of the New York Post earlier this week and admitted that it’s a hot topic of conversation with his teammates. “I talk to [Nolan McLean] all the time about it, and he had some good talks with Skubal when they were in the [World Baseball Classic] together,” Thornton told Puma. “It would be awesome to bounce ideas, especial
item.content:encoded:
The prospect of Tarik Skubal becoming the Mets’ next big free-agent signing is already dancing in the head of some members of the organization.
Zac Thornton spoke with Mike Puma of the New York Post earlier this week and admitted that it’s a hot topic of conversation with his teammates.
“I talk to [Nolan McLean] all the time about it, and he had some good talks with Skubal when they were in the [World Baseball Classic] together,” Thornton told Puma. “It would be awesome to bounce ideas, especially coming from another left-handed pitcher. Sean [Manaea] and I talk a lot, just about being lefties — there are not many around here, so it would be awesome to have another powerhouse left-handed pitcher around here.”
Even with a young core of promising arms like McLean, Thornton, Christian Scott, and Jonah Tong, president of baseball operations David Stearns made it clear in his end-of-season availability that “it is necessary for us to add to our rotation.”
Skubal would provide the bona fide veteran ace Freddy Peralta never became after his half season in Queens—though he certainly looks the part with the Tampa Bay Rays, who are battling the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS.
Regardless, the left-handed Skubal will be the crown jewel of the free agent market this winter. The two-time defending American League Cy Young Award winner was dealt from the Detroit Tigers to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the trade deadline and remained his dominant self, going 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 1.048 WHIP.
Over his last three seasons, Skubal is 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA and 655 strikeouts in 546 innings pitched.
With a lockout looming, which could potentially carry a salary cap that will limit player salaries, Skubal will likely sign quickly — and that deal will be historic. He is projected to sign the richest contract for a free-agent pitcher ever, which should exceed $300 million.
Whether Stearns would be intrigued by doling out such an offer might not be as cut-and-dry as many might initially think.
Yes, the Mets’ president of baseball operations has had an aversion to handing out long-term big-money contracts to pitchers, which is understandable given the fragility of many major-league arms and the seemingly never-ending onslaught of injuries that come with it.
Skubal himself missed a month earlier this season when he had to undergo surgery to remove loose bodies from his pitching elbow.
But Stearns has gone to the negotiating table with a big-money contract offer for a starting pitcher while with the Mets. He offered Yoshinobu Yamamoto a 12-year, $325 million deal in December of 2023, but the Japanese superstar took an identical deal to join the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Skubal would certainly fit the mold of coaxing such an offer from Stearns, especially if it means that the Mets are that much closer to legitimate contention in 2027, if there is baseball.

item.content:encoded:
山本由伸との「１２球・７分間」の熱闘の２日後、今度は１１球粘って逆転２ラン…バウアーズの粘り腰
完了しました
米大リーグのポストシーズン（ＰＳ）ナ・リーグ優勝決定シリーズ（４戦先勝方式）は１４日（日本時間１５日）の第３戦で、ブルワーズ（中地区１位）がドジャース（西地区１位）を６－２で破って３連勝とし、ワールドシリーズ進出に王手をかけた。
六回に１－２と逆転されたブルワーズは七回表無死一塁で、５番のバウアーズが好投を続けていたドジャース先発のスネルからファウルで粘って１１球目を右翼席に放り込み、この逆転２ラン本塁打が決勝弾となった。
バウアーズの殊勲の伏線は２日前の試合にあった。１２日（同１３日）の第２戦の三回、この試合で４番に入っていたバウアーズは、２走者を置いた場面でドジャースの先発、山本由伸に対して１２球粘って四球を選び、チャンスを広げて続くイエリチの逆転２点適時打を呼び込んだ。
この打席、バウアーズはフルカウントからファウルで６球粘り、緩急を織り交ぜる山本の多彩な投球にくらいついた。ＭＬＢ公式ページによると、１２球の対戦に要した時間はおよそ７分間。球数がかさんだ山本は逆転打を喫したこの回途中に７５球、３失点で降板し、間違いなく試合の流れを変えるシーンとなった。
今年３１歳のバウアーズは２０１３年のドラフト７巡目、全体２０８番目でパドレスに指名された。１８年にメジャー昇格し、ブルワーズが５球団目。主に一塁と外野を守り、ブルワーズ３年目の今季はレギュラーシーズンでメジャー自己最多の２６本塁打を打っている。（デジタル編集部）

item.title: [Orange County Register] Brewers push Dodgers to the brink, hit 3 homers off Blake Snell for 3-0 NLCS lead
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

The plucky little team that doesn’t hit home runs hit three of them off of Blake Snell on Wednesday night. The Milwaukee Brewers handed the Dodgers a 6-2 defeat in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, pushing the back-to-back champions to the brink of elimination with the possibility of a sweep to avenge the one the Dodgers handed them last year. “It’s a pretty simple answer,” Max Muncy said when as
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Reach out and feel the drywall. The Dodgers’ backs are up against it.
The plucky little team that doesn’t hit home runs hit three of them off of Blake Snell on Wednesday night. The Milwaukee Brewers handed the Dodgers a 6-2 defeat in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, pushing the back-to-back champions to the brink of elimination with the possibility of a sweep to avenge the one the Dodgers handed them last year.
“It’s a pretty simple answer,” Max Muncy said when asked how the Dodgers find themselves in this position. “We’re playing like (profanity). They’re playing great. It’s as simple as that. No need to overcomplicate it.”
Dreams of a three-peat on life support, the Dodgers’ thoughts now have to be on a ‘four-peat’ – it will take four consecutive victories for them to become just the second team in MLB history to come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven series. The 2004 Boston Red Sox (featuring a key stolen base by a reserve outfielder acquired at midseason from the Dodgers) did it in the American League Championship Series against the New York Yankees.
“If we lose, we’re done. We’ve got to go on one-game winning streaks four games in a row,” Kike’ Hernandez said.
“At the beginning of this year, we set out to do something historic,” Muncy said. “It looks like we’re going to have to make a little more history along the way if we want to accomplish that. That’s the task ahead of us. We still have the pitching staff to be able to do it. We just have to get some hits. If we can back our pitching staff then I know that, like I said, we have the pitching staff to do it.”
Tyler Glasnow is scheduled to start Game 4 on Thursday and try to save the Dodgers’ season. Muncy is correct — Glasnow won’t be able to do it without someone applying paddles to the Dodgers’ flatlining offense.
The Dodgers might not be going down without a fight. But so far, they are going down without any of the things it takes to make an offense successful in the postseason.
They are 2 for 16 with runners in scoring position in this series, 3 for 32 in the postseason. They have just two two-out hits in the three NLCS games (both singles) and only two extra-base hits (both doubles). The Dodgers hit 204 home runs in the regular season (tied for fourth in the National League) and eight more in their four-game National League Division Series victory over the Atlanta Braves (the most in the postseason to that point). They have hit none in the NLCS.
“They’re really good pitchers,” Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard. They’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too many opportunities to build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They trust their stuff in the zone. With all three fastballs, with a lot of guys that have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball, it’s really hard to kind of put barrels on the ball. So you’ve got to build some momentum that you can create with hits, but we haven’t been able to get a big hit.”
The Brewers have grabbed any momentum right back from the Dodgers. The Dodgers have scored in just five of the 27 innings so far. Four of those five times, the Brewers responded by scoring in the next half-inning themselves.
It happened again to turn Game 3.
Snell hadn’t give up a home run this year but Jackson Chourio sent the first pitch he threw Wednesday into the right-field pavilion. Snell thoroughly dominated the Brewers through six innings after that. He retired 18 of 20 batters after Chourio’s home run, striking out nine. Through the first five innings, the Brewers swung at 32 of Snell’s pitches and missed (17) more times than they made contact.
But the Dodgers’ lifeless offense did nothing against the Brewers’ second consecutive rookie starter, Robert Gasser, who held them scoreless on three hits and a walk through five innings.
Brewers manager Pat Murphy went to his bullpen after that, calling on Abner Uribe for the seventh time in their seven postseason games. When Uribe took the mound, the Brewers’ relievers had pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings in the NLCS and had allowed just one earned run in 28⅔ innings this postseason.
But Uribe walked the bases loaded, retiring just one batter. That brought up Will Smith – 1 for his first 25 this postseason. Smith jumped on a first-pitch fastball from Uribe and lined it off the wall in left-center field for a two-run double and a 2-1 lead.
It was the kind of clutch hit that Smith has provided time and time again over the years and had the stadium rocking.
Murphy made his next move, bringing in left-hander DL Hall with runners at second and third. Hall struck out pinch-hitter Kiké Hernandez and Tommy Edman as the Dodgers failed to capitalize on a chance to break the game open.
Snell went back out for the seventh inning having retired 14 in a row. But he walked Andrew Vaughn to start the inning and bring up Jake Bauers whose 12-pitch walk in the third inning of Game 2 was a critical turning point against Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He did it again, extending his at-bat against Snell for 11 pitches and sending the last one, a fastball over the heart of the plate, into the right-field seats for a two-run home run. Two pitches later, Snell floated a changeup over the middle and Garrett Mitchell sent it on the same flight path as Bauers’ drive.
In 1,200⅔ career innings (regular season), Snell has only given up 15 home runs to left-handed hitters. Bauers and Mitchell did it back-to-back. The Brewers hit 154 home runs during the regular season, the fewest in the National League. They have outhomered the Dodgers 5-0 in the NLCS.
“I mean three home runs in a game — I didn’t give up one the whole year,” Snell said. “To have three in a game is pretty frustrating.”
The Brewers added single runs in the eighth and ninth innings to pull away.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers' Muncy, Pages Named 2026 Gold Glove Finalists
item.dc:creator: Jordon Lawrenz

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to avoid being swept in the National League Championship Series, and that starts in Game 3, which takes place on Wednesday, the same day when the Gold Glove Award finalists were revealed.
The likes of Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, Kyle Tucker, and even Yoshinobu Yamamoto weren't named finalists, but Andy Pages and Max Muncy were.
Pages represents the Dodgers in center field while Muncy is their third base representative.
Both players have their work cut out for them, but even being named one of three NL finalists is a huge accomplishment for how grueling a 162-game season is.
Dodgers face stiff odds for Muncy to win
Muncy is officially a Gold Glove finalist for the second time in his career, but it seems like he's going to need to try again next year.
The three-time All-Star is matched up against Alex Bregman, one of the best defenders in all of baseball, and Javier Sanoja.
MLB.com made note that Muncy hasn't been a plus defender by fielding run value since 2021, and that's something that Bregman has been doing on a consistent basis.
Here in 2026, Bregman notched his seventh straight season of being an above-average defender, and the 2024 Gold Glove Award winner ended the year with +9 outs above average.
For reference, that was second among all third basemen. Sanoja has a case to be made with his +6 OAA, which is fourth in the NL, along with his +5 FRV, which was tied for fourth.
Sanoja won the Gold Glove Award last year as a utility player, but now is stuck at third base where both he and Muncy will likely fall to Bregman.
Pages is stuck against Pete Crow-Armstrong
Is there a worse person to be going up against than Pete Crow-Armstrong? The likely 2026 NL MVP had a defensive value worth +23 runs, which led the league.
PCA's OAA came in at +26, which is officially the highest by an outfielder in a single season this decade.
Pages sported a strong +13 FRV, which was the third most among qualified outfielders, but it was still nothing in comparison to Crow-Armstrong's +26.
Sure, Pages led the league with 14 outfield assists, but it seems like a foregone conclusion that PCA will be leaving with the hardware on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Michael Harris II was the third finalist. He put together a career year with his +14 OAA and +12 FRV.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are two games away from being eliminated at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
With right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto having pitched in Game 2, the current state of affairs is far from where fans expected the Dodgers to be as the series heads back to LA. The 2025 World Series MVP lasted just 2.2 innings on Monday in an uncharacteristic one-strikeout performance, but there was still tons of baseball to be played after his exit.
After left-hander Alex Vesia finished off the third inning with four pitches, one of last year's October standouts in Roki Sasaki trotted out to the mound to face the Brewers in the fourth.
Sasaki's October success last season, especially in multi-inning spots, is partially why manager Dave Roberts was in a position to explain himself for only having Sasaki out to throw one frame.
The man who opened up the bottom of the fifth inning for LA, southpaw Kris Bubic, recorded just two outs on 22 pitches, one of which was turned into a solo home run for Brewers catcher William Contreras to tie the game.
Despite Sasaki's resume, Roberts went with the left-hander, but revealed he was looking for far more than two outs from the former All-Star.
"To me, you're trying to cover six-plus innings," Roberts said. "For me, I felt Bubic had four out of five left-handed hitters, and that's a perfect spot for him. I knew they weren't going to for him, and you got Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you've got a great spot for Bubic. Tries to go with the fastball up to Contreras and then hits a homer.
"That's a decision I made, and we just didn't — again, that's his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero."
After Bubic walked a batter to leave a man on first and second, Brock Stewart came in to end the inning. Instead of a fresh arm coming in for the bottom of the sixth, Stewart remained in the game. Three batters later, Contreras was back up to bat with a tie game, two on and one out.
Contreras hit the first pitch he saw 76.9 mph into the outfield grass to give his team the lead and Stewart was removed from the contest. Tanner Scott entered the game after him and promptly struck out the next two batters to get out of the inning.
Roberts was asked about why Stewart was in instead of Scott entering against an already hot Contreras.
"It just felt like trying to put Contreras on the ground," Roberts said. "Contreras didn't hit the ball hard. He flared it out to left field, drove in a run, and that's what they do."
Roberts continued to point out the differences between the kind of at-bats that the Brewers' brand is a byproduct of.
"I think for me just in total they saw a ton more pitches than we did," Roberts said. "They had much better at-bats than we did across the board top to bottom, and then they put the ball in play, created havoc, and that's what they do, and we didn't do that.
"That's the difference in the game. I think that there's certainly a lot to unpack, but they did what needed to do tonight."

item.title: [Brewer Fanatic] A Different Kind of Challenge: How Can Brewers Beat Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow?
item.dc:creator: Jake McKibbin
item.description: Brewers Video Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are the Dodgers' near-immortal October heroes. After most teams start a series with hurlers like that, there's a major step down in quality to the back half of their rotation. In Los Angeles's case, though, that step is much smaller. Here's how the Brewers can attack the other two-time Cy Young Award winner in the Dodgers rotation, and one of the most physically intimidating pitchers in baseball. Projected Game 3 Starter: Blake Snell The Brewers
item.content:encoded:
Brewers Video
Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are the Dodgers' near-immortal October heroes. After most teams start a series with hurlers like that, there's a major step down in quality to the back half of their rotation. In Los Angeles's case, though, that step is much smaller. Here's how the Brewers can attack the other two-time Cy Young Award winner in the Dodgers rotation, and one of the most physically intimidating pitchers in baseball.
Projected Game 3 Starter: Blake Snell
The Brewers got a first-hand look at just how good Snell can be in 2025. He capitalized on a change in his pitch mix, throwing a heavy dose of in-zone changeups that completely befuddled Milwaukee in one of the best starts of his career: eight innings, one hit, 10 strikeouts. But that isn't always the version of Snell that opponents see.
Snell is willing to nibble around the edges of the zone, making swing decisions in the shadow zone particularly important for Milwaukee against another high-release, left-handed pitcher with a devastating fastball and changeup. The difference is that Snell is much more comfortable giving up a walk than Skubal, and somehow even harder to square up when hitters do swing.
His start against the Braves showed both sides of that equation. Snell lasted just 3⅔ innings, walking five hitters and striking out five, but he allowed only one run. Three hits and five walks might suggest that Atlanta simply missed its opportunity, but there is a reason Snell can survive that kind of traffic. His fastball has elite ride, and when he works at the top of the zone, it's extremely difficult to get on top of. Add a wicked slider and curveball that blend beautifully with the fastball from his high release point, plus a quality changeup, and Snell's four-pitch mix is loaded with ways to beat a hitter.
This is the type of contact quality Snell has allowed this season:
Snell isn't overly concerned about the walks, because he trusts his ability to strand runners once they reach base. Especially in the tense environment of a playoff game, he can induce chase, generate swing-and-miss, and force weak contact when hitters finally do get the ball in the zone.
Even when he does throw strikes, Snell is difficult to hit. Fresh off the injured list, his fastball has gained roughly an inch of both ride and run compared with 2025. As a result, the one pitch that hitters had previously been able to barrel with some consistency has taken a step forward.
That makes this a waiting game for Milwaukee. Can the Brewers build enough pressure on Snell that he finally blinks before they do? Can they turn the walks and deep counts into hard contact when he eventually has to come into the zone? More importantly, can they force him to throw enough pitches that the Dodgers have to turn to their bullpen earlier than they'd like?
Atlanta managed to run Snell's pitch count up and get him out of the game, and white-knuckled their way to a win from there. Milwaukee may need a similar approach. They're unlikely to drop the hammer on Snell, and they'll need some batted-ball fortune when their opportunities arrive, but if they can make him work, accept the walks and punish the mistakes, they have a path to turning Snell's greatest strength, his willingness to live on the edges, into a weakness. Braves batters swung at just 34 of the 90 pitches Snell threw in the NLDS. To match that patience in last year's NLCS Game 1, the Brewers would have had to swing 10 fewer times. The key to beating Snell is those 10 fewer swings.
NLCS Game Four Starter: Tyler Glasnow
Tyler Glasnow works from one of the highest release points in baseball, pairing a high-velocity fastball with breaking balls that feature sharp, late movement. Like Snell, he's comfortable working outside the strike zone and using his secondary pitches to induce chases. His two breaking balls can fall off the table, making them difficult to touch—let alone hit hard.
Glasnow threw just 74 innings during the regular season, but posted a 0.95 WHIP and a 34% strikeout rate, a testament to how difficult he is to handle—particularly when he gets ahead in the count. There is, however, another dimension to the matchup. Glasnow can be vulnerable to the running game: opposing runners went 14-for-17 on stolen-base attempts against him in 2026, an 82% success rate. If the Brewers can get men on base, they may have opportunities to pile on pressure with their legs. The bigger question, of course, is how they get on in the first place.
Once again, the fastball could be the key. Glasnow's breaking balls have enough depth and movement to make consistent contact a challenge, particularly when hitters are forced to protect against them outside the strike zone. The Brewers will need to recognise those pitches early and avoid expanding the zone. The encouraging sign is that, unlike Yamamoto, Glasnow has shown a more conventional relationship between count leverage and pitch selection: as he falls behind, the likelihood of seeing a fastball increases.
Glasnow's outing against the Braves offered a glimpse of both his vulnerability and his ability to limit the damage. He struggled to locate his secondary pitches, walking five hitters, and threw his four-seam fastball in the strike zone roughly two-thirds of the time. The Braves managed just one run, however, illustrating how difficult it can be to capitalize on Glasnow's occasional command issues.
Even when Glasnow loses his feel for the secondaries, his four-seamer remains a formidable weapon. Released from a high arm slot, the pitch can play above the barrel, but it also cuts just enough to slide along the barrel. That helps him limit hard contact and keep the ball in the park, even when hitters know a fastball is coming. The offering has some similarities to the one the Brewers recently faced from Nick Pivetta, against whom they timed the fastball well. That being said, recognizing the pitch and actually squaring it up are two very different things.
The Brewers' best approach will be to make Glasnow work. Extending at-bats, laying off pitches outside the zone, and forcing him to find the strike zone with his secondary offerings could create opportunities to get runners aboard. From there, they can look to apply pressure on the bases and turn a difficult matchup into a more uncomfortable one. That fits their broader approach of building pressure and forcing mistakes, but Glasnow is unlikely to unravel simply because the Brewers make him work.
Ultimately, the Brewers will need to combine disciplined at-bats with timely hitting. Glasnow has the stuff to overpower even a patient lineup, and he would be an ace in most postseason rotations. The opportunity is there, but exploiting it will require the Brewers to turn the few openings he gives them into meaningful damage.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers return home in a 2-0 hole against the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
The Dodgers swept the Brewers last year in the NLCS, but Milwaukee has shown that it won’t go quietly this time around.
Milwaukee won a close battle in Game 1 by a final score of 2-1 before chasing Yoshinobu Yamamoto early in Game 2 in a 7-4 victory.
The Dodgers now return home, where they’re 52-31 this year, while the Brewers are 49-34 on the road.
It’s a southpaw showdown in Hollywood for Game 3 on Wednesday night.
Here are the odds, probable pitchers, and predictions for Brewers vs. Dodgers Game 3 on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Brewers vs. Dodgers Odds, Run Line and Total
Run Line
- Brewers +1.5 (-156)
- Dodgers -1.5 (+129)
Moneyline
- Brewers +148
- Dodgers -180
Total
- 7.5 (Over -106/Under -114)
Brewers vs. Dodgers Probable Pitchers
- Brewers: Robert Gasser (5-5, 3.87 ERA)
- Dodgers: Blake Snell (4-1, 1.90 ERA)
Robert Gasser threw four one-run innings against the Dodgers in his first postseason start this year. That run came on a solo home run, one of three hits by the Padres in a 3-1 Brewers victory.
Blake Snell lasted just 3.2 innings in his playoff start against the Braves, allowing one run on three hits with five walks and five strikeouts.
Brewers vs. Dodgers How to Watch
- Date: Wednesday, Oct. 14.
- Time: 8:00 p.m. ET
- Venue: Dodger Stadium
- How to Watch (TV): FS1
- Brewers record: 103-59 (5-1)
- Dodgers record: 100-62 (3-3)
Brewers vs. Dodgers Best MLB Prop Bets
Dodgers Best MLB Prop Bet
- Blake Snell UNDER 1.5 Earned Runs (-133)
Blake Snell has been terrific since returning from the injured list in early August. He allowed five runs in 39.2 innings (1.13 ERA) in his final eight regular-season starts, yielding one run or fewer in all eight outings.
The veteran southpaw then allowed just one run in his start against the Braves in the NLDS.
The Brewers weren’t as good on the road this season, and Snell has been lights out no matter where he’s pitching. In fact, Snell allowed just one run in 18 innings in three starts at Dodger Stadium after returning from the IL.
Brewers vs. Dodgers Prediction and Pick
The Brewers were able to maintain their home-field advantage in the first two games of the series, and I think the Dodgers will get a win at home in Game 3.
This is where the Dodgers’ depth really shows. Blake Snell would be the Game 1 or at least Game 2 starter for most teams, but Los Angeles’ acquisition of Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline pushes the veteran southpaw to Game 3 at home.
Robert Gasser has been better than people think for Milwaukee, but I’m not too sure he can go toe-to-toe with Snell. And if the Brewers get a lead, the Brewers would be smart to save their best bullpen arms for the rest of the series.
It is a big price for the Dodgers at -180, though, which is why I’m recommending the run line as my best bet. If you want to just take the moneyline, that’s fine too, but I don’t like giving out best bets at this high of a number.
Pick: Dodgers -1.5 (+129)

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Brewers news: Brandon Woodruff update, Shohei Ohtani benching decision, Blake Snell's pre-start comments
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas

The Brewers, who will send Robert Gasser to the mound first in Game 3, are not taking wins in Games 1 and 2 of the NLCS for granted, knowing that the script can quickly be flipped with Dave Roberts' star-studded squad manning the opposing dugout.
