item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman knows exactly how he wants to spend the Dodgers’ five-day break before the National League Division Series.
It’s all about his swing, and getting it right for the playoffs.
Freeman spoke at length Tuesday about his late-season struggles, the work he plans to put in during the bye and why he feels confident he can get his swing where it needs to be by Saturday. He also talked about the Dodgers’ October experience, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and the example set by his father after the death of Freeman’s mother when he was a child.
Five Days to Work on the Swing
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing. I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple months.
“I have a plan I’m going in with, and hopefully that will take care of itself throughout the course of the week where I’ll be in a good spot by Saturday.”
Freeman dealt with knee trouble during the second half, but he put the responsibility for his drop in production on himself.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well. I just didn’t play well the last couple months of the season. That’s what I’m going to go with.
“Did I have some ailments with my knees? Yes, I did. I don’t know how much that attributed to it subconsciously, trying to do stuff where it didn’t hurt as much. There were times during the course of the last couple months where there would be a three- or four-day span where the knee was a problem and I couldn’t get into the front side, so maybe I created bad habits.
“But I won’t blame it on that. I just played bad.
“My knee’s in a good spot now. That’s why the bye week is huge for me personally. I’ve got five days to really work on the mechanics of my swing, and my knee’s in a good spot where I feel like I will be able to do that.”
Freeman planned to hit on the field every day, using batting practice to work through the changes before seeing live pitching later in the week.
“Today is going to be a big day to see how BP goes. I feel like BP’s probably not going to go well today just because of how my swing is right now, and then I’ll be able to start working on it.
“If I am blocking balls to left field in BP, then I can make those adjustments. There’s a lot going on in this head a lot of times, but it’s going to be big because I’m going to hit BP every single day on the field.
“I think that will help, seeing balls velocity-wise, to be able to start moving it lower and lower and down toward the shortstop. Hopefully that will get my body in line with how I want it to work going into Saturday.”
Back to Something That Worked in 2024
The physical picture is far better than it was during another recent October.
“A couple Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse ailment-wise. I truly feel good right now physically, so it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days.
“I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Freeman said he currently has no pain in the knee and expects rest after the season to be enough heading into next spring.
For now, he is going back to a swing thought that worked during the Dodgers’ 2024 championship run.
“It’s all evolved. Today I am going to kind of get more into my legs, and I’m going to try what I used in the World Series in ’24, kind of the step-out thought, so I’m not bending over and cutting off my swing.
“That’s the thought going into today. I’m very confident that’s going to help get things back in line throughout the course of the week.”
The bye also gives Freeman something he rarely gets during the season: time to work on a change without having to test it in a game a few hours later.
“I think the rest kind of takes care of itself mentally. I think that’s more of the mental rest.
“Physically, we’ll go out there and practice today, then we’ll play in some sim games the next two days and practice again. It’s baseball. You’ve got to play every day.
“But I think it’s more of the mental rest of not trying to figure out how to do something each and every day. That’s what’s going to be beneficial to me, where I can work on something today, go into tomorrow, work on something, then see how it translates into the live at-bats against real pitchers.
“It’ll be nice to work on something in BP and not have to take that into a game two hours later and see if it works. Today I can hone in on what I want to do in BP, and that’ll be it.
“Tomorrow I’ll come into BP and do that again, so I’ll have at least 400 swings going into tomorrow’s live BP of hopefully kicking out some of the bad habits.”
NLDS First, History Later
The Dodgers enter October with a chance to win their third straight World Series, but Freeman said his focus is much smaller right now.
“Personally, I’m thinking about the NLDS and whoever we play and getting ready for that.
“I think if you think big picture in this moment, you lose sight of some things. You’ve just got to take it one day at a time.
“We do understand the bigger picture, but if you’re looking at the bigger picture, you won’t be able to get to that big picture if you’re not focusing on the now.”
The Example Freeman Got From His Dad
One of Freeman’s more personal answers came when he was asked where his habit of taking responsibility and pushing through tough stretches came from.
Freeman pointed to his father, Fred, who raised three boys after Freeman’s mother, Rosemary, died when Freddie was 10.
“What I learned from my dad is someone who had his world turned upside down when my mom passed away when I was 10 years old, and he continued to take care of three boys and work and do the best he possibly could day in and day out and not be a ‘woe is me’ person.
“Obviously when I’m 10, I’m not thinking about that stuff. But as I’ve gotten older and I look back at what that man had to go through, the flip of a switch he had, he was a single dad of three and had his own business with his brother and still continued day in and day out to be the person he is and take care of us.
“As I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized there are no excuses. That man had every excuse in the book to do whatever he wanted in 2000, and he didn’t make an excuse. He went out there and did it each and every day.
“That’s my dad. Was he hard on me about my grades? Yeah, because I wasn’t that great in school. But he’s the best dad I probably could have had in that situation, with what he was going through and what we were all going through.
“What you think of him as a very down-to-earth man, that’s who my dad is. He’s a blessing.”
Plenty of Faith in Yamamoto and the Dodgers’ Staff
Freeman also had high praise for Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the right-hander heads into his third postseason with the Dodgers.
“He is special. From the first live BP that I saw when I faced him, it’s just special stuff, special command, the poise on the mound. Nothing’s too big for him.
“He’s one of those special pitchers that we get to watch day in and day out. It feels like he can put the ball wherever he wants, and we are very confident whenever he goes out there.
“Our pitching staff is pretty special, in my opinion. We’ve got four number ones rolling out there. It just goes on and on. Our pitching staff is most likely going to do it again like they did last year, and hopefully our offense can pick it up this year.”
Experience Counts in October
The Dodgers once again enter the postseason with one of baseball’s older position-player groups. Freeman sees the years this roster has spent playing deep into October as something that can help now.
“We’ve started in February overseas the last couple years and ended up winning the World Series. We know what’s going to be happening in the playoffs. We know what’s going to be thrown at us, the atmospheres.
“I think experience is huge in this. We’ve played a lot of baseball. We’ve been together a long time. We know what it takes.
“I think experience is definitely on our side going into this.”
For Freeman, though, the first order of business remains the same one he laid out at the start of the interview.
Five days. A healthy knee. Plenty of swings.
And a chance to get everything lined up before Saturday.

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA. One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Mets should make all-out Tarik Skubal pursuit, but it could take a philosophical shift
item.dc:creator: Danny Abriano
item.description: As the Mets enter the offseason, they'll be facing a familiar challenge: put together a team that can get them back to the playoffs for the first time since 2024. David Stearns and the front office failed in that regard last offseason, due in part to the drastic changes that were made to the roster and coaching staff. item.content:encoded:
As the Mets enter the offseason, they'll be facing a familiar challenge: put together a team that can get them back to the playoffs for the first time since 2024.
David Stearns and the front office failed in that regard last offseason, due in part to the drastic changes that were made to the roster and coaching staff. There were other things at play, including long-term injuries to Francisco Lindor and Clay Holmes, some worst-case scenarios playing out, and an over-reliance on bounce backs.
This time around, the Mets will almost certainly have much less turnover, but that doesn't mean the overall result in 2026 wasn't an abject failure.
New York had a 34-31 record after the All-Star break, which was a big improvement after things spun out of control in the first half and led to a trade deadline sell-off.
But the most important developments for the Mets after their dismal start? The emergence of Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing, the impressive return of Christian Scott, the moxie and performance of Zac Thornton, and some good late-season signs from Jonah Tong.
The above should give the Mets confidence that they're in solid shape when it comes to their lineup and a chunk of the starting rotation. They have an emerging young core to complement their more established stars, and potentially have high-upside players coming soon from the upper levels of the minors. But serious help is still needed this winter.
Specifically, the Mets need to add external help at first base, address the DH spot, bolster the bullpen with multiple new arms (including a back end option), and -- most importantly -- find a pitcher who profiles at the very top of the rotation.
In both 2025 and 2026, the Mets were done in, due in large part to not having enough starting pitching depth. And it can be argued that they left themselves short one legitimate starter both times. That can't happen again, so New York should be focused on pairing a new prospective ace with another addition who profiles in the middle or back of the rotation.
About that ace ... it's not difficult to figure out that it should be Tarik Skubal.
In one of the weakest free agent classes in recent memory, Skubal stands out even more than he ordinarily would.
Fresh off back-to-back Cy Young awards, the 29-year-old Skubal posted a 2.72 ERA (2.51 FIP) and 0.96 WHIP while walking just 1.5 per nine innings and striking out 186 batters in 158.2 innings in 2026.
Skubal's season was briefly interrupted by NanoScope surgery on his pitching elbow that kept him out of action from April 30 through June 13. But he continued to be dominant upon his return. After having a 2.70 ERA (2.11 FIP) over his first seven starts, Skubal had a 2.73 ERA (2.66 FIP) in the 19 starts he made post-surgery, with 10 of them coming after he was dealt to the Dodgers at the trade deadline.
During Stearns' end-of-season news conference on Monday at Citi Field, he was asked multiple times about the Mets' offseason plan for adding pitching, but unsurprisingly didn't offer much when asked in a roundabout way about a possible Skubal pursuit.
"I do think it is necessary for us to add to our rotation," Stearns said. "We can do that in a variety of different ways. We've talked about this plenty before -- you'd always love to add to the top of your rotation, any team would love to do that -- over the long term, what we need to do is develop pitchers at the top of our rotation, and I think we are proving we can do that, and we'll continue to do that."
While Stearns refused to make any declarations about the type of pitcher the Mets would go after, it is pointless to read into that.
For one, Skubal is still under contract with the Dodgers, and no executive is going to talk about going after a player who is on another team.
Second, and even more importantly, no exec is going to tip his or her hand entirely and risk wrecking leverage ahead of possible negotiations.
While Stearns (smartly) won't say it, I will: The Mets should make Skubal the centerpiece of their offseason plan, using the resources at their disposal to add one of the most talented pitchers in the sport to slot in front of Nolan McLean.
The Mets' biggest need this offseason is at the top of their rotation, with Skubal a nearly perfect way to fill that need. And Skubal will cost only money, since the midseason trade from Detroit to Los Angeles makes him ineligible for a qualifying offer and the draft pick compensation it would've required from any team that signed him.
When discussing Skubal and the Mets, it's obviously instructive to consider Stearns' philosophy when it comes to signing pitchers to long-term deals. Specifically, he has not shown much interest in signing pitchers in their late-20s or 30s to those kind of pacts -- and that philosophy is generally a valid one.
For every long-term, big-money deal to a pitcher 29 or older that works out (Max Scherzer's seven-year deal with the Nationals looks incredible in retrospect, and the Yankees' deal for Max Fried is aging well), you can point to a whole bunch that didn't or currently aren't (Patrick Corbin, Jacob deGrom, Jordan Zimmermann, Felix Hernandez, Corbin Burnes).
As far as how Stearns has operated in the past, it's fair to throw what he did in Milwaukee out the window given the payroll constraints he was working under.
But except for a serious pursuit of then-25-year-old Yoshinobu Yamamoto ahead of the 2024 season, Stearns' main forays into the free agent starting pitching market with the Mets have been measured:
Sean Manaea: Three years, $75 million
Clay Holmes: Three years, $38 million
Frankie Montas: Two years, $34 million
Luis Severino: One year, $13 million
Griffin Canning: One year, $4.25 million
Of those signings, Holmes was the biggest success as the Mets turned him back into a starter after he spent years in relief. But that success resulted in Holmes being set to opt out after the second season of his contract, which led to New York trading him at the deadline.
During his time leading the Mets' baseball operations, Stearns has been reluctant to offer deals to starting pitchers (except Yamamoto) that exceed three years. When that is your philosophy, the risk is obviously lower. But sometimes a calculated risk is needed.
When it comes to Skubal, there is risk. In addition to the minor surgery he had this season, Skubal underwent flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and had Tommy John surgery in 2017.
Skubal is also likely to receive the biggest deal ever for a starting pitcher when it comes to average annual value. Maybe his age (30 when next season begins) and yearly value of his deal will make the years easier to stomach, but something like $400 million for eight years is easy to imagine.
There's also the looming lockout and new CBA to consider.
While it's difficult to envision the players caving on a hard salary cap, it's fair to believe the new CBA will include stiffer penalties for teams that exceed the luxury tax thresholds.
But even after considering all of that, it's still reasonable to conclude that the Mets should go after Skubal with gusto -- that he should be the exception to Stearns' rule, maybe with a slight nudge from owner Steve Cohen.
Things could always go sideways, as they often do with long-term deals for older starting pitchers. But there's no reason to think Skubal won't be exceptional for the first half of any deal he signs, which would also theoretically line up with a World Series window the Mets will hope to be entering.
When you look at Skubal, who combines one of the best arsenals in baseball with perhaps the best command in baseball (and whose metrics look like this), the biggest risk for the Mets would be not going all-in on him.

item.content:encoded:
JustPredictions
Justice editors predict the upcoming year of sports.
Ben Khayat ’28: Only one Big Ten team will make the College Football Playoffs. The sample size is small, but the Big Ten has been downright shameful to start the 2026 season. The obvious examples are the Michigan Wolverines coming back from the dead to prevent a home loss to the Western Michigan Broncos, and the Rutgers Scarlet Knights succumbing to the UMass Minutemen, a team that didn’t win a single game last season. The rest of the conference hasn’t been much better. The Oregon Ducks came into the season ranked #2 in the country, but came up limping in their one-score win over the Boise State Broncos before getting dispatched by Oklahoma State on Saturday. The Ohio State Buckeyes led 23-3 against the Texas Longhorns, only to allow 21 unanswered points and choke what would have been the first statement win the conference has had this season. Come January, I can’t imagine many of these “top” teams will have impressed anybody enough to get an at-large bid over some other power conference opponents.
Luca D. Jordan ’28: The Chicago Bears will make the Superbowl this season. After having an amazing breakout season under head coach Ben Johnson and making their first playoff appearance since 2020, the Chicago Bears have shown explosive growth with a new offensive direction. Defined by their comeback wins, the Bears almost clinched the semi-finals last season, but quarterback Caleb Williams threw a bad pass that led to an interception against the Los Angeles Rams. Despite an unfortunate play that ended his season early, Williams has shown flashes of an all time great quarterback. When it comes down to the last few seconds, Williams is known to perform herculean throws to save the game. Although their offseason wasn’t particularly exciting, expect a surprising surge in performance across the board from the entire roster. Previous champs Seattle Seahawks are dead in the water without Sam Darnold and the Rams have added some big names to their roster, but it’s just stars over substance. The Bears have a few decades of an underdog legacy behind them, and that’s too much destiny to ignore.
Bryan Wolfe ’27: The New York Knicks are running it back! I have faith. Even though the Philadelphia 76ers have the starting five of doom and despair, I believe in the king of New York Jalen Brunson to lead us back to the promised land.
Chava Thiell ’29: Alexander Zverev will finish the 2026 ATP season with an ATP finals win and the World #1 ranking. As unfortunate as it may be for diehard Sincaraz fans, Jannik Sinner isn’t healthy and Carlos Alcaraz is still adjusting to his return to tennis after a four-month hiatus. After Zverev clinched two Slams this year, his momentum cannot seem to be stopped. Conversely, I think Aryba Sabalenka will walk away with the WTA Finals trophy, inspired by a heartbreaking US Open final loss to rival Elena Rybakina and a mission to come away from the season with a big tournament win.
Eli Sandalow ’28: The New England Patriots will go 4-13. Drake Maye looks like he regressed, AJ Brown is prone to long-term injuries and Rhamondre Stevenson is one of the most overrated running backs in the NFL right now.
Alyssa Wu ‘29: The Dodgers won’t three-peat this year.The Dodgers have a stacked lineup, with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, plus a star-studded starting rotation of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Along with their veterans, new acquisitions this year include stars like Tarik Skubal, a two-time American League Cy Young winner. Despite this, the Dodgers have not dominated through the season as many expected. They went 13-14 in August, though they have found their footing again in September. Injuries raise more concerns; Ohtani only returned to the lineup on September 23 after a stint on the injured list and is not expected to pitch for the remainder of the season. Reliever Blake Treinen, who has helped bring three championships to the Dodgers in his six seasons, suffered a season-ending injury on September 26. With Kyle Tucker and Andy Pages being the only starting position players under the age of 30, the question is whether these Dodger veterans will be healthy and as productive as they used to be during the postseason. The MLB Playoff bracket itself does not always reward the ‘best’ team. The Dodgers in 2022 are one of the clearest examples of this. In 2022, they went 111-51 and won 14 of 19 regular-season games against the Padres. However, after winning Game 1 of the NLDS, they lost three straight to the San Diego Padres, ending their season. The postseason can bring plenty of surprises, and a team’s regular season does not always predict its success in the playoffs. The Dodgers had to come back from a 3-2 deficit to win last year’s World Series, and this year’s team seems to be much more vulnerable. The Dodgers are sure to make it far in the playoffs, but another championship is far from guaranteed.

item.content:encoded:
Eight Dodgers on Monday were nominated for Major League Baseball’s All-MLB teams, an honor that has existed within the sport since 2019.
Fan voting for the honor will take place beginning Monday through Friday, October 9, with that fan vote counted alongside “a decorated panel of media members, broadcasters, former players and other officials throughout the game” in determining first and second All-MLB teams.
Shohei Ohtani is one of six nominees at designated hitter, Mookie Betts is one of 11 shortstop nominees, and Freddie Freeman one of 14 nominees at first base. All five have captured All-MLB honors in five previous years, with Ohtani collecting first-team All-MLB honors at DH in each of the last three years and four of the last five, plus second-team DH in 2022, to go with his two first-team All-MLB honors (2022-23) and one second-team All-MLB honors (2021) as a starting pitcher.
Betts is a four-time first-team All-MLB outfielder plus a second-team honor in 2019. Freeman has two first-team honors at first base, the last coming in 2023, and three second-team honors.
Max Muncy is one of 11 third baseman vying for All-MLB honors, looking for his first All-MLB selection, facing an uphill battle with Rays star Junior Caminero among those nominated at the position.
Andy Pages is the only Dodger among the 24 outfield nominees, seeking his first All-MLB selection.’
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who garnered first-team All-MLB honors last year, and Tarik Skubal, a first-teamer in each of the last two years, are the two Dodgers starting pitchers nominated at starting pitcher this year.
Tanner Scott is one of 20 relief pitchers up for All-MLB honors.
All-MLB teams will be announced during the MLB awards show on November 11, which will begin at 5 p.m. PT on MLB Network.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers don't have a designated playoff closer. That isn't as bad as it sounds
item.dc:creator: Bill Shaikin
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott. - Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon. SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win t
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

item.title: [MLB.com] Snell shows he's ready to reprise role in LA's postseason rotation behemoth

item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- When Blake Snell took the mound for the final time in the regular season on Saturday afternoon, he eased any lingering concerns the Dodgers may have had after the southpaw exited his previous start with left groin tightness.
The Dodgers wanted to see Snell make close to a full start in order to feel good about him taking the ball going forward, but they weren't going to push him. So Snell's outing was finished after he had thrown four innings on 77 pitches (50 strikes), allowing one run on five hits while striking out three Giants.
The Dodgers had initially hoped to have Snell pitch five innings, but he was not at his sharpest, having thrown only one inning in the past two weeks due to his groin issue. But it was better to brush the rust off now than in the postseason.
"Really encouraged by it, and just happy to get my legs underneath and get going and completely move past the groin," Snell said. "I mean, it felt great today, and the velo was good. And was inconsistent -- I’ve got to figure my body out a little more, but I got a week to do so, and I'm really looking forward to that."
Limited to only nine regular-season starts by left shoulder fatigue, loose bodies in his left elbow and the groin issue, Snell is not only determined to get back to where he was last postseason, when he recorded a 3.18 ERA through six outings (five starts). He wants to continue to grow.
"I want to be better than what I was last October. I think I can definitely do that," Snell said. "But we all need each other. I think that's the biggest thing."
Snell's status had been the primary concern surrounding L.A.'s daunting four-man postseason rotation that also features Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow. Now that Snell has made his final regular-season tuneup, the main question for the Dodgers is how to line up their starting four for the NL Division Series, which begins on Oct. 3 at Dodger Stadium.
"I think as a pitching staff, we're going to be OK," said Kiké Hernández, who hit a game-winning solo homer in the top of the ninth inning. "So it's up to the offense to do what we're capable of doing."
There is a compelling case for each of those four starters to be the ace in any given rotation in the Majors. The Dodgers feel good about any of them making a Game 1 start, so the decision essentially comes down to how they can get the most out of their starting four.
"To be honest with you," Roberts said, "you could put them all in a hat, and you could make a case for any order you put them in."
One consideration is rest. The Dodgers ran a six-man rotation for most of this season, meaning their starters are accustomed to five days' rest. Yamamoto has not started a game on less rest than that -- although he did pitch on back-to-back days to clinch MVP honors in last year's World Series. Skubal, Snell and Glasnow all have experience pitching on four days' rest.
Here's what that could mean for the NLDS, when the Dodgers can reset their rotation to their liking: Yamamoto starting Game 1 would allow him to start a potential Game 5 on his usual rest. Skubal, Snell or Glasnow could start Game 2, then be available for a potential Game 5 on four days' rest.
It may also be on the table for whoever does not start Games 1 and 2 to be available out of the 'pen, like in last year's NLDS, when Glasnow pitched 1 2/3 innings in relief in the series opener before starting Game 4.
The aim for the Dodgers, Roberts said, is to "maximize those four guys," who are the strength of their pitching staff.
"We're only as good as our starters," Snell said. "And I love our starters, I love the staff, the way we push for each other to be great and support each other. … It's what we've all been waiting for, and now it's time to prove it. It's an important time for us."

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers loom large over upcoming CBA negotiations, with owners gunning for a salary cap while players battle to maintain maximum earning potential. The Dodgers, in active pursuit of their third-straight World Series title, own MLB's highest payroll at $380.5 million. That includes $30 million-plus allocated to Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Tarik Skubal and Mookie Betts on an annual basis.
The Dodgers' ability — and willingness — to outspend opponents, sometimes almost four-to-one, has frustrated fans and given cheaper owners an excuse to cry foul. While the Dodgers experienced their share of turbulence this season, this team clearly isn't going anywhere. Their profits more than make up for their expenses. Look no further than jersey sales:
MLB's top 10 jersey sellers in 2026
The Dodgers have four of the top-10 jersey sellers in MLB this season. That does not include marquee names like Kyle Tucker (acquired last offseason), Tarik Skubal (acquired at the trade deadline) or their other two-time Cy Young winner, Blake Snell.
| Player | Team |
|---|---|
| 1. Shohei Ohtani | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 2. Aaron Judge | New York Yankees |
| 3. Pete Crow-Armstrong | Chicago Cubs |
| 4. Ronald Acuña Jr. | Atlanta Braves |
| 5. Fernando Tatis Jr. | San Diego Padres |
| 6. Freddie Freeman | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 7. Bryce Harper | Philadelphia Phillies |
| 8. Mookie Betts | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 9. Yoshinobu Yamamoto | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| 10. Juan Soto | New York Mets |
In 2025, the Dodgers became the first team in baseball history to generate over $1 billion in gross revenue. While owner Mark Walter's financial troubles made headlines in recent weeks, his troubles are concentrated in the business world, not the baseball world. The Dodgers are an unequivocally profitable venture; not the sort Walter is likely to relinquish any time soon.
There's a reason the Dodgers are willing to spend on premium free agents every winter. It's not because Walter loves baseball and wants to win. Perhaps that is a part of the equation, but baseball, now more than ever, is a business. And the vast majority of ownership groups view it through that cold, inflexible lens. The Dodgers spend money to make money. They fill out the stadium, sell jerseys and rake in merchandise money from all across the globe. Their roster's strong international presence, spearheaded by Shohei Ohtani and his fellow countrymen, plays no small part in that.
Also helpful: so much of L.A.'s salaries are deferred. Ohtani is making $2 million per season through the duration of his contract. He's making the same money as an unproven third-year player still under arbitration.
The Dodgers' dominance will press on — with or without a salary cap
The Dodgers are not going anywhere. Even with a salary cap. It's a sobering truth, but one all 29 opposing fanbases must accept, lest their dreams be shattered further on down the line.
That's not to say the Dodgers are unbeatable. They will eventually fall in the postseason, perhaps as soon as next month. Plenty of great organizations find ways to build competitive rosters without approaching $400 million in spending. Conversely, a high payroll does not guarantee success. Ask the last-place New York Mets, whose $349 million payroll ranks second in MLB, behind only L.A.
Los Angeles is certainly a unique case study, however. Not only are the Dodgers willing to spend, but stars clearly want to play for them. There's the allure of Hollywood. The desire to play for a world-class organization, with top-notch facilities and a great support staff. There is also, more plainly, the desire to win championships. No team in recent history is more consistently in the World Series mix than Los Angeles.
Moreover, the Dodgers just know how to run a successful organization. That is overly broad and simplistic, but it's the truth. Beyond their high-paid stars, L.A. has the best farm system in baseball, with six prospects in MLB Pipeline's Top 100. And that's after trading two top-100 prospects for Tarik Skubal. L.A. has the depth of talent behind their stars to consistently trade for upgrades at positions of need — or to develop cheaper stars to backfill "holes" in their expensive lineup.
While a salary cap would limit L.A.'s ability to sign the Shohei Ohtani, almost their entire core is locked up for the foreseeable future. Those who aren't (see: Skubal) would no doubt love to re-sign. If MLB puts a cap on deferred money, sure, that'll impact their future plans. But Los Angeles would gladly spend more money upfront. Only $30 million of Kyle Tucker's $240 million contract last winter was deferred. The Dodgers managed to sign the offseason's most prized free agent despite longer-term offers from the Mets and Blue Jays, two big-market clubs with competitive aspirations of their own. The Blue Jays had just taken L.A. seven games in the World Series.
Los Angeles has the talent and the flexibility to navigate whatever comes next. If the players win out and no salary cap is implemented, it will be business as usual. If MLB owners get their way, L.A. can maneuver around forthcoming changes — even shed major salaries — without falling far in the standings. The Dodgers have the prospect depth and development staff of a well-run, small-market club, paired with the outsized expenses of the glitzy team from L.A. That is how you build sustainably.
The Dodgers are designed to survive just about anything at this point.

item.title: [Friars on Base] Padres found their postseason blueprint in win over Dodgers' Yoshinobu Yamamoto

item.content:encoded:
Wednesday night's game was quite telling for the San Diego Padres. Facing the two-time defending World Series champions in Los Angeles, the Padres were able to do something that seldom occurs: Defeat a Dodgers ace.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto has owned San Diego this season. Entering Wednesday night, he had given up three earned runs in three starts (20 innings) against the Padres this season. But the Friars played their game to a different tune a fourth time around.
They gritted out at-bats. They stole three bases. Manny Machado had a timely home run. En route to a 5-1 road victory, the Padres tagged Yamamoto for four runs (two earned) on Wednesday. It still wasn't a bad outing for Yamamoto, but it took him 88 pitches to get through six innings, which is opposite of his usual efficiency.
This game was a potential glimpse into what the Padres are capable of doing in October. They will face plenty of strong pitching in the playoffs, but can they apply the pressure in each at-bat, as well as on the bases? If so, then we can strap in for an exciting Padres postseason.
Padres don't need much from their starting rotation if everyone else applies pressure
What's especially interesting about San Diego's win over the Dodgers on Wednesday was that Robbie Ray was pulled after recording 10 outs. If your ace is getting yanked in the fourth inning, it usually spells trouble, particularly on the road against a dynamite team like the Dodgers.
Rather, San Diego played to their strengths. On top of timely hitting and working deep into counts, the Padres' bullpen was lights out once more. Of course, you do not want five relievers pitching in every postseason game, but in games like this one, the Padres showed they can win regardless of how well their starter does.
Jason Adam is back. Mason Miller and Adrián Morejón make up an intimidating back-end duo. Yuki Matsui and Bradgley Rodriguez are reliable middle-innings guys. That's where the Padres will outrun the competition, in the bullpen. But, if the rest of the team can wear down the opposition like they did on Wednesday, there's no reason that San Diego can't make a run in October.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers' three-peat hopes rest on their four aces — and bottom-of-order production
item.dc:creator: Bill Shaikin
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers’ path to a third straight World Series title will depend on four frontline starters, but manager Dave Roberts hopes his offense won’t leave them carrying the load. - In a 2-0 win over San Francisco, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages offered a timely reminder that the Dodgers will need consistent production from the bottom half of the lineup in the playoffs. - Hernández is a proven October hitter, while Pages is finding his swing after c
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers’ path to a third straight World Series title will depend on four frontline starters, but manager Dave Roberts hopes his offense won’t leave them carrying the load.
- In a 2-0 win over San Francisco, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages offered a timely reminder that the Dodgers will need consistent production from the bottom half of the lineup in the playoffs.
- Hernández is a proven October hitter, while Pages is finding his swing after coming back from a broken hand.
SAN FRANCISCO — This is the 60th anniversary of the 1966 World Series, in which the losing team did not score for the final 33 innings of the series.
That losing team was the Dodgers. Over the final three games of the series, Jim Palmer, Wally Bunker and Dave McNally of the Baltimore Orioles each pitched a complete-game shutout.
That art of pitching is not in style today. Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched two complete games last October, but he cannot pitch every game, even if he left that impression upon the Toronto Blue Jays.
The Dodgers’ clearest and cleanest route to a three-peat nonetheless rests upon the four shoulders of Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. If the four aces can do to October opponents what the 1966 Orioles did to the Dodgers, or some reasonable 21st century facsimile, we’ll see you at the parade.
Does Dodgers manager Dave Roberts believe his starting pitchers will have to carry the load in October?
“I hope not,” Roberts said.
Tarik Skubal gives up just three hits and strikes out 10 in his final start before the postseason to help carry the Dodgers to a 2-0 win over the Giants.
Friday’s 2-0 victory over the San Francisco Giants offered two encouraging swings. Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages each hit home runs, a reminder that a properly tuned Dodgers offense runs on more than Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Will Smith.
Skubal scattered three hits and struck out 10 in seven scoreless innings, which would have gone for naught without the Hernández and Pages home runs. Given that the Dodgers were playing the Giants and the remains of their depleted roster, it was something of a warning sign: this could happen against a postseason team.
No team can plan to score a lot of runs against the Dodgers’ starters. The opposing game plan would be to neutralize them and keep the game close enough to where one or two big swings can make the difference. The Giants, who have the National League’s second-worst record, almost pulled it off.
“When you get to the postseason, they’re going to try to eliminate Shohei and try to make other guys beat you,” Roberts said. “So it always sort of comes to the middle to the bottom of the order, where you’ve either got to get guys on base or get hits, get big hits.”
In October, Hernández is who you want at bat. He has homered in six of the seven postseason series he has played for the Dodgers, including each of the last five. In 33 postseason games for the Dodgers, he has driven in 25 runs.
For most players, offensive production drops in October, when batters face the best pitchers from the best teams. For Hernández, his career OPS is .796 in the regular season and .792 in the postseason.
And, for all his summer struggles, he is batting .354 this month, with an OPS just shy of 1.000. He’ll be, as the league-issued hoodies used to say, October ready.
For Pages, however, last October was cruel.
This October was not looking particularly promising, either. Pages missed 27 games because of a broken hand, leaving him the final six games of the regular season to get his swing back into rhythm.
“You think that you take five weeks off,” Roberts said, “that your timing is going to be off a little bit.”
So far, so good: five hits in 12 at-bats, including the home run Friday.
Pages ended the regular season last year with four hits in his final 28 at-bats. That, Roberts said, tells him this October will be different for Pages.
“I think the one thing is the confidence, how he went into last October really scuffling, and it sort of bled into October,” Roberts said, “where I think right now he feels really confident, swinging the bat well, and the hope is that this one bleeds into October as well.
“So, I think it’s definitely a different result going into October, and then also his headspace. There’s a lot more confidence this year.”
In 2025, when the Dodgers won the World Series, they ranked second among the 30 major league clubs in runs scored, and in home runs. In 2024, when they won the World Series, they ranked third in runs scored, and in home runs.
The Dodgers rank fourth in runs scored this year, and seventh in home runs. The offense is down some, if not much. In all the national postseason hype, the Dodgers projections will boil down to one sentence: Can anyone stop those starters?
“I think at first glance that’s what you see in our ballclub,” Roberts said. “But we have a lot of talented, really good hitters and I hope they work hand in hand and not just our pitching and defense carry us.”
For the Dodgers, the postseason opens one week from Saturday. If the Dodgers roll out the 1966 playbook, their October stay will be short.

item.title: [MLB.com] Skubal cruises before Sasaki, Scott prep for postseason roles
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO -- Tarik Skubal was showing no signs of slowing down in what was shaping up to be his most dominant start as a Dodger. But after throwing seven scoreless innings on 75 pitches, the southpaw was shaking hands and receiving hugs in the visitors' dugout at Oracle Park. item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Tarik Skubal was showing no signs of slowing down in what was shaping up to be his most dominant start as a Dodger. But after throwing seven scoreless innings on 75 pitches, the southpaw was shaking hands and receiving hugs in the visitors' dugout at Oracle Park.
Skubal struck out 10, gave up just three hits and faced two batters over the minimum in his final regular-season start on Friday night.
His pitch count was in such a good spot that he could have made a bid for the second "Maddux" of his career. But when the bottom of the eighth inning came around, Skubal remained in the dugout and Roki Sasaki relieved him on the mound.
“That was the best we’ve seen," manager Dave Roberts said. "He was on a mission tonight. You could see it. Everything was working. He just went after those guys and did a fantastic job."
While Roberts has maintained that the Dodgers won't approach their final games of the season differently with the No. 2 postseason seed locked in, the 2-0 win over the Giants was an example of how having nothing left to play for changes the calculus of in-game decisions.
With five days off before the NL Division Series begins on Oct. 3 at Dodger Stadium, Roberts isn't necessarily looking to use this weekend for load management. But these final games are the Dodgers' last opportunity to try out players in their postseason roles in a lower-stakes environment.
Had this game taken place a week ago, Skubal may have stayed in to finish off his gem. But the Dodgers had already planned on having Sasaki pitch on Friday, and with only two additional games remaining for him to prepare for his postseason bullpen role, they opted not to deviate from that plan.
Sasaki got his work in, tossing a 1-2-3 eighth inning with two strikeouts in his second appearance back from the injured list. Tanner Scott closed out the victory, the Dodgers' 98th of the season -- which could be a hint at how both leverage arms will be used in the postseason.
"It’s better to have as many guys as you have confidence in in leverage," Roberts said. "So it just allows us to deploy guys whenever we need to."
For much of Skubal's two months as a Dodger, both he and the team maintained that they had not seen him at his best on the mound. Not only was Friday his best performance yet with L.A., but it came against a team that had frustrated him just six days earlier.
Last Saturday, Skubal lasted only five innings while allowing four runs against the Giants at Dodger Stadium. He bemoaned his lack of fastball command, which he believed was the main factor behind the disappointing results.
Skubal didn't just have command of his fastball on Friday. He had command of everything, throwing 60 of his 75 pitches for strikes and going 21-for-23 in first-pitch strikes. He generated 21 whiffs on 43 swings (48.8%), including a season-high 12 on his fastball.
"I think it's the key to who I am. I think it makes me who I am," Skubal said. "I don't know how many pitches I threw tonight, but felt like there were only like 14 or 15 balls out of however many throws. … I'm not going to do that every time, but I think that just speaks to conviction and the pitch-calling."
Said Giants manager Tony Vitello: "He’s going to come right at you, so maybe we could have been a little more aggressive early. But the bottom line is, he was sharper than the other night [in L.A.], and maybe we weren’t as sharp."
While Skubal received minimal run support -- solo homers from Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages in the second inning -- he had no issues holding the line.
Along with Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, Skubal is part of the four-man gauntlet the Dodgers will run out in October. In his final tuneup, he looked postseason-ready, and then some.
"Once the months change and the playoffs start, nothing matters," Skubal said. "It's just about winning that game, and that's how I treat every single start. Because I'm just trying to put our team in a position to win a baseball game, and that won't change from today and whenever my next start is."

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers news: Blake Snell sets the record straight on lil bro dynamic with Tarik Skubal appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Blake Snell has had enough of the confusion. The Dodgers left-hander joined the broadcast booth during Friday's game against the Giants and used the airtime to settle a running clubhouse debate with Tarik Skubal, who has been calling him the younger of the two.
"We got to get this right, you know, it's a lot of comments and people don't know who big bro and little bro is," Snell said in the middle of the game. "I'm big bro. Little bro's right there."
Blake Snell trying to set the record straight on who is big bro and lil bro with Tarik Skubal 🤣🤣🤣 pic.twitter.com/SAMX7Vdwg5
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
— Dodgers Nation (@DodgersNation) September 26, 2026
He then turned his attention to the man on the mound. "You never know what he's gonna say," Snell said. "Little bro, he's a crazy guy. But he's throwing cheese right now."
Snell has the math on his side. He turns 34 in December, while Skubal is 29, making the older-brother claim fairly straightforward. That has not stopped Skubal from insisting otherwise.
The dispute went public after the Dodgers clinched the NL West on Sept. 17 with an 8-2 win over the Reds. Amid the celebration, Skubal made his own declaration on camera. "This is my best friend," he said. "He's my little brother."
The two have leaned into the bit hard since Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Tigers at the trade deadline. They have pulled pranks on each other in the clubhouse, knocked over each other's chairs, and traded Step Brothers-inspired jokes on social media. Skubal recently posted an AI-generated video of the pair rapping Migos' "Hotel Lobby," captioned simply with a reference to his "lil bro."
That post drew attention beyond the joke. Skubal is set to become an unrestricted free agent this offseason, and Dodgers fans have read his comfort in the clubhouse as a sign he may want to stay. He has gone 4-2 with a 2.95 ERA across nine starts since the trade.
Snell, meanwhile, is working his way back after leaving a start against Cincinnati with left groin tightness. Both are expected to anchor a postseason rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto, with Tyler Glasnow also in the mix if health allows.
Whatever the birth order, Los Angeles will take both of them in October.
Related: Dodgers set to receive huge Dalton Rushing boost right before playoffs

item.content:encoded:
ドジャースでワールドシリーズ3連覇を狙う大谷翔平。
32歳になったスターは、このほど故障者リストから復帰した。23日は1安打、24日には2安打を放ち、復調に向けて歩みを続けている。
そうしたなか、MLBは2026年のユニフォーム売上ランキングを発表。
大谷は2010年の集計開始以降で、4年連続売り上げ1位となった史上初のMLB選手になった。
「大谷の人気は、新たな高みに達した。2010年に集計が開始されて以来、メジャーリーグで初めて4シーズン連続で『最も人気なユニフォーム選手』になったのだ。2023年以降、アメリカ、日本、そして世界中で最も多くのユニフォームを売り上げている」とのこと。
9位には山本由伸（ロサンゼルス・ドジャース）、20位には村上宗隆（シカゴ・ホワイトソックス）も入った。
野球界最高の人気選手である大谷は、復帰後に確かな復調を見せている。
パドレス戦ではMLB屈指のクローザーであるメイソン・ミラーが投じた時速102.6マイル（約165キロ）の速球を捉えた。
水曜には384フィート（約117メートル）、木曜にも382フィート（約116メートル）の大飛球をかっ飛ばし、木曜日の平均打球初速は101.9マイル（時速164キロ）を記録した。
『LA Times』は「大谷は故障者リストから復帰後、力強い打球を放ち、ストライクゾーンの見極めも向上させるなど、好ましい兆候を見せている。もし膝と上腕二頭筋の怪我を完全に克服したのなら、ドジャースがワールドシリーズ3連覇に挑む上で重要な役割を果たすはず」と伝えている。
また、デーブ・ロバーツ監督も「今後の兆しであってほしいね」と期待を口にしていた。
筆者：井上大輔（編集部）
画像提供：Getty Images

item.description: 土曜未明…大谷翔平の“BIGニュース”「ものが違う」 副収入196億円も納得「本当に凄い」 MLBがユニホーム売上ランキングを発表 メジャーリーグ機構（MLB）と選手会は25日（日本時間26日）、「MLBショップ」などにおける今季開幕戦以降のユニホーム売上ランキングを発表し、ドジャースの大谷翔平投手が4年連続で1位に輝いた。土曜未明に駆け巡った快挙に対し、日本のファンは「本当に凄いわ」と鼻高々だった。 MLBの発表によると、追跡調査が開始された2010年以降、4年連続で首位を守った選手は大谷が初だという。大谷はエンゼルス時代から圧倒的な人気を誇ったが、名門ドジャース移籍後にさらに加速。ポストシーズンにも進出したことで、全米での知名度も飛躍的に上昇した。 日本未明の午前2時頃の“最新発表”に対し、日本人ファンからは歓喜と称賛の声が殺到した。「さすがユニコーン」「ユニホーム売上1位は世界一の選手と言う証でしょう」「4年連続ってスゴイな」「引退しても一定数売れそう」「やっぱり大谷翔平はものが違うんだよ」「4年連続1位は凄いね」「人気も実力もNo.1」と誇らしげなコメントが並んだ。 大谷は過去
item.content:encoded:
土曜未明…大谷翔平の“BIGニュース”「ものが違う」 副収入196億円も納得「本当に凄い」
MLBがユニホーム売上ランキングを発表
メジャーリーグ機構（MLB）と選手会は25日（日本時間26日）、「MLBショップ」などにおける今季開幕戦以降のユニホーム売上ランキングを発表し、ドジャースの大谷翔平投手が4年連続で1位に輝いた。土曜未明に駆け巡った快挙に対し、日本のファンは「本当に凄いわ」と鼻高々だった。
MLBの発表によると、追跡調査が開始された2010年以降、4年連続で首位を守った選手は大谷が初だという。大谷はエンゼルス時代から圧倒的な人気を誇ったが、名門ドジャース移籍後にさらに加速。ポストシーズンにも進出したことで、全米での知名度も飛躍的に上昇した。
日本未明の午前2時頃の“最新発表”に対し、日本人ファンからは歓喜と称賛の声が殺到した。「さすがユニコーン」「ユニホーム売上1位は世界一の選手と言う証でしょう」「4年連続ってスゴイな」「引退しても一定数売れそう」「やっぱり大谷翔平はものが違うんだよ」「4年連続1位は凄いね」「人気も実力もNo.1」と誇らしげなコメントが並んだ。
大谷は過去4度のMVPに輝いているだけでなく、「フォーブス」によるとグラウンド外での収入1億2500万ドル（約196億円）は全アスリート1位に立っているという。
2位にヤンキースのアーロン・ジャッジ外野手、3位に「40-40」達成のカブスのピート・クロウ＝アームストロング外野手が続いた。さらに日本勢では、ドジャースの山本由伸投手が9位、今季メジャーデビューを果たしたホワイトソックスの村上宗隆内野手が20位にランクイン。トップ20に日本人選手3人が同時に入る史上初の快挙となった。
（Full-Count編集部）

item.content:encoded:
Redacción Deportes, 25 sep (EFE).- El japonés Shohei Ohtani, estrella de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, volvió a ser el jugador con la camiseta más vendida de las Grandes Ligas, una posición que ocupa por cuarto año consecutivo, según la lista publicada este viernes por MLB y MLB Players, Inc. (Mlbpi).
Ohtani se convirtió así en el primer jugador desde que MLB comenzó a registrar las ventas en 2010, que encadena cuatro temporadas como líder en comercialización de camisetas.
PUBLICIDAD
Desde 2023, los aficionados han comprado la camiseta Nike de Ohtani más que cualquier otra en Estados Unidos, Japón y el resto del mundo, consolidando al jugador japonés como la figura con mayor demanda comercial entre los peloteros de las Grandes Ligas.
El listado, elaborado a partir de las ventas de camisetas Nike realizadas a través de Fanatics, incluido MLBShop.com, desde el Día Inaugural de la temporada 2026, sitúa al capitán de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Judge, en el segundo puesto y al jardinero de los Cachorros de Chicago Pete Crow-Armstrong en el tercero.
PUBLICIDAD
Crow-Armstrong, quien esta temporada se convirtió en el séptimo jugador en la historia de las Mayores y el primero de los Cachorros en conectar al menos 40 jonrones y robar 40 bases, alcanzó el mejor puesto para un jugador de Chicago desde que el puertorriqueño Javier Báez fue tercero en 2018.
El listado también refleja la presencia de otras figuras de alcance internacional. El venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr., de los Bravos de Atlanta, ocupa el cuarto lugar, seguido por el dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., de los Padres de San Diego.
Los Dodgers colocaron a tres jugadores entre los diez primeros, con Ohtani al frente, Freddie Freeman en el sexto puesto y Mookie Betts en el octavo. El japonés Yoshinobu Yamamoto, también de Los Ángeles, aparece noveno.
La temporada 2026 marcó además un registro inédito para los jugadores japoneses, con tres de ellos entre los 20 primeros de la clasificación, después de que el toletero Munetaka Murakami, de los Medias Blancas de Chicago, debutara en el vigésimo puesto.
PUBLICIDAD
Yamamoto, por su parte, ocupa el noveno lugar, mientras que Ohtani mantiene el liderazgo de una clasificación que vuelve a poner de manifiesto su dimensión dentro y fuera del terreno de juego.
La lista se conoce antes del inicio de las Series de Comodines de ambas ligas, que comenzarán el próximo martes 29 de septiembre, con Ohtani, Judge y Crow-Armstrong entre las principales figuras de unos equipos que ya tienen asegurado su boleto a la Postemporada. EFE
PUBLICIDAD

New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge was second for the second straight season, MLB and the players' association affiliate MLB Players, Inc. said Friday. Judge finished third in 2023 and '24. Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Ch
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Shohei Ohtani has become the first player to lead Major League Baseball jersey sales at the end of four straight seasons since the sport started tracking figures in 2010, among four players in the top 20 on the two-time World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers.
New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge was second for the second straight season, MLB and the players' association affiliate MLB Players, Inc. said Friday. Judge finished third in 2023 and '24.
Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs was third, up from 16th at the end of last season, and Atlanta's Ronald Acuña Jr. was fourth, an increase from 11th last year.
San Diego's Fernando Tatis Jr. was fifth, followed by the Dodgers' Freddie Freeman, Philadelphia's Bryce Harper, the Dodgers' Mookie Betts and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and the New York Mets' Juan Soto.
Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox was 20th, and he joined with Ohtani and Yamamoto to become the first trio of Japanese players in the top 20.
Texas' Corey Seager was 11th, followed by Toronto's Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Boston's Adley Rutschman, the Phillies' Kyle Schwarber, Pittsburgh's Paul Skenes, Seattle's Cal Raleigh, Cincinnati's Elly De La Cruz, San Diego's Jackson Merrill and Arizona's Nolan Arenado.
MLB's list tracked sales on Fanatics' sites, including MLBShop.com, since opening day.
___

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Freddie Freeman on Finding his Swing in the Nick of Time
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman believes he’s finally beginning to rediscover his swing, and with the Dodgers having secured a first-round bye into the NLDS, the veteran first baseman is encouraged by what he’s seeing from his teammates as October approaches. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman believes he’s finally beginning to rediscover his swing, and with the Dodgers having secured a first-round bye into the NLDS, the veteran first baseman is encouraged by what he’s seeing from his teammates as October approaches.
Freeman collected two hits in Thursday night’s 4-1 loss to the Padres, both coming after he made an adjustment during his third plate appearance. He explained afterward that he’s starting to feel more comfortable using his lower half, something that had been missing from his swing during his recent struggles.
“I know the last couple of at-bats, a little better. Got more in my legs,” Freeman said. “So, trying to make adjustments pitch to pitch. Just trying to get a feel, and felt something on a foul ball in my third at-bat.”
“Took it into the next couple pitches, got a hit. Took it into the next at-bat, got a hit. So I’ll take it into tomorrow.”
Getting Hot at the Right Time
Although the Dodgers dropped the final two games of their series against San Diego, Freeman is encouraged by the individual performances he’s seeing throughout the lineup, particularly from Shohei Ohtani and Mookie Betts.
“I’m just encouraged with Shohei getting a couple of hits, Mookie staying hot,” Freeman said. “That’s really what it’s all about. Guys getting hot right now.”
“We got the first-round bye, so play some good baseball this weekend and take it into next week.”
Freeman also praised Ohtani’s return to the lineup, including the hard contact he made against Padres closer Mason Miller during Wednesday’s game.
“It’s nice for Shohei to come out there and get some hits. That ball off Mason Miller was special, so I know that would feel good for him,” Freeman said.
“Mookie’s been hot. Teo’s been swinging the bat great. Will’s been really good lately, too. So a couple of us can add on to it, and Kyle, obviously, he’s been really good the last month, too. So we’ve got a good stretch going.”
The first baseman also provided a reassuring update about his own health. Asked about the condition of his knee, Freeman offered a simple response.
“Knee’s good. I feel nothing.”
When asked whether the issue was now yesterday’s news, he confirmed that it was.
“Yeah. Yeah. All good.”
Freeman Isn’t Concerned About the Dodgers’ Record Against Playoff Teams
One of the more interesting exchanges came when Freeman was asked about the Dodgers’ struggles against quality opponents during the second half of the season.
Since their series victories over the Yankees and Phillies, the Dodgers have struggled to win series against teams with winning records, including the Padres, who took two of three at Dodger Stadium this week.
Freeman, however, isn’t particularly interested in revisiting those results.
“I wouldn’t have even known unless you guys asked,” he said. “All we care about is playing good this weekend, these three games, and take that in.”
“It doesn’t matter who we’re playing on Saturday or what we’ve done against those teams. It’s all out the window from Saturday. It’s game on there, but playing good baseball is a good option. Positive things going into the off week.”
It’s an understandable perspective from a veteran who knows that regular-season results offer little comfort once the postseason begins. The Dodgers will certainly have to start producing more runs against elite pitching staffs, but Freeman’s focus is on getting the entire lineup clicking when the games matter most.
A Well-Earned Opportunity to Rest
Freeman also emphasized the importance of the first-round bye, particularly for a team that has endured the physical demands of another long season.
“I think rest for all of us is always nice,” he said. “We’ve been grinding since February, getting ready for the season. Then you go through a 162-game schedule. It’s a lot.”
“So we played really good baseball for six or eight months, and we get rewarded for that. So we’ll take it in and rest up and get ourselves ready to go for Saturday.”
With several key players having returned from injuries in recent weeks, the opportunity to rest and prepare rather than immediately enter a Wild Card series could be especially valuable.
Four Number One Starters
Perhaps Freeman’s most emphatic response came when a reporter referred to another member of the Dodgers’ rotation as the team’s number four starter.
Freeman wasn’t having any of that.
“We have four number one starters. That’s what we have,” he said. “I don’t think anybody is going to be one, two, three or four. They’re all ready to go, and whatever role they’re going to be deployed in the NLDS, we got four starters.”
“So I think our guys, we got four number ones. If you want to call him a number four, you can call him a number four, but they’re all number ones.”
It’s a sentiment that should resonate with Dodger fans after watching the recent performances of Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow. The starting rotation appears to be coming together at an ideal time, and Freeman clearly has confidence in the arms that will be taking the mound in October.
For now, Freeman’s priorities are straightforward: carry his recent improvements into the final weekend, get the rest he’s earned, and prepare for the NLDS.
And if a few more Dodgers can find their swings along the way, all the better.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
The AL and NL Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie begins Tuesday, Sept. 29 with many of MLB’s most popular players preparing to take center stage. Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Aaron Judge of the New York Yankees and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs are leading the league in most popular player jerseys as their respective Clubs enter the final weekend of the regular season with Postseason berths secured.
Ohtani’s popularity reached new heights as he became the first player to finish four straight seasons with the most popular player jersey in the Majors since tracking began in 2010. Since 2023, fans have purchased Ohtani’s Nike jersey more than any other in the U.S., Japan and worldwide. With Dodgers teammate and reigning Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s jersey ranking no. 9 and Chicago White Sox All-Star slugger Munetaka Murakami debuting on the list at no. 20, this is also the first season that three MLB Players from Japan have their jerseys in the top 20.
After becoming only the seventh player in MLB history and first Cubs player to hit at least 40 home runs and steal at least 40 bases in a single season, Crow-Armstrong’s jersey finished as the third most popular of the season – the highest ranking for a Cubs star since Javier Báez finished third in 2018.
This list, released jointly today by MLB and MLB Players, Inc. (MLBPI), accounts for sales of Nike jerseys from the Fanatics network of sites, including MLBShop.com, since Opening Day of the 2026 Championship Season.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have punched their ticket to the postseason and will be looking to three-peat.
Last postseason, Yoshinobu Yamamoto had a run for the ages, throwing two complete games, working 28 2/3 innings and closing out the World Series on zero days of rest after throwing six innings the day before. He won World Series MVP and will once again be looking to deliver in October.
Yamamoto was an All-Star once again this year, posting a 2.53 ERA. However, he let Dodgers fans know after his final start of the regular season that he plans to play his best baseball in the postseason.
"Now we're getting into October, so I'd like to live up to the high expectations," Yamamoto said after Wednesday's game.
The Dodgers' postseason rotation this year will feature Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. It's very possible that Yamamoto is not even the Dodgers' No. 2 starter in October. The Dodgers have yet to reveal how they will line up their starters in October, but it's very likely they will have a bye and will have their pick.
If Yamamoto delivers as he did in last year's postseason, the Dodgers will have no problem winning the National League once again.
More MLB: Rays Announce Two-Time All-Star Not Available For ALDS

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres are facing off in the rubber match of their three-game series on Thursday night with plenty at stake for both teams.
The Dodgers, who have already won the National League West division, can clinch a first-round bye with a win or Atlanta Braves loss over the season's final four games.
They're also still chasing the Milwaukee Brewers for the No. 1 seed, but will need some help to secure home-field advantage throughout the postseason.
As for the Padres, they're looking to clinch a postseason spot, with their magic number currently sitting at 1.
Thus, the winner of Thursday's game will be celebrating in some capacity. If it's the Padres, they'll be making a champagne and beer mess in the visitor's clubhouse at Dodger Stadium. If it's the Dodgers, they'll be shaking hands and looking forward to their five-day layoff beginning next week.
Dodgers vs Padres Pitching Matchup on Thursday
Right-handed pitcher Tyler Glasnow is taking the mound for the Dodgers in his final tune-up before the postseason.
Glasnow has been shaky since coming off the injured list at the end of August, sporting a 4.50 ERA over 28 innings with 38 strikeouts to 10 walks. Overall this season, he's 5-1 with a 3.46 ERA and 87 strikeouts across 67.2 innings (12 starts).
Glasnow is expected to be the team's No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
Opposite Glasnow will be Padres right-hander Nick Pivetta, who missed nearly five months this season with an elbow injury but has been incredibly sharp since returning.
In his three starts since coming off the IL, Pivetta has allowed just three runs over 14 innings for a 1.93 ERA. He has 11 strikeouts to one walk in that time.
