Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger ov
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns.
- Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question.
Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger over the postseason availability of several other MLB difference-makers as October approaches.
Here is a look at the injury status and hopeful returns of impact players on playoff qualifiers and contenders:
American League East
Tampa Bay Rays: Acquired from Baltimore at the trade deadline, swingman Tyler Wells posted a 1.50 earned-run-average before right forearm tightness sidelined him. He is back solely pitching from the bullpen, and could be a key piece for the Rays in their surprising surge to the division title.
Hopeful return: Slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls is recovering from a right hip flexor strain and signs point to him returning by October.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
New York Yankees: The return of staff ace Fried is huge for a team that has clinched a wild-card berth and remains a long step behind the Rays for a division title and first-round bye. The left-hander out of Studio City Harvard-Westlake High gave up one run while walking none over seven innings in his longest start in almost five months. Fried has had two arduous IL stints dealing with a bone bruise on his left elbow.
Hopeful returns: Giancarlo Stanton or Trent Grisham returning in October would give the Yankees lineup additional pop. Three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge has been back for a week since missing more than three months with a fractured rib.
Boston Red Sox: A right quadriceps strain has kept All-Star center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela sidelined for two weeks. However, Rafaela told NESN that he expects to be activated this weekend, a substantial addition to a team that likely will play the Yankees in wild-card series.
Hopeful return: A year ago, Garrett Crochet was 18-5 and led the AL with 205 1/3 innings pitched. This year, left shoulder inflammation and a lat strain have kept him sidelined since April. However, he has ramped up bullpen sessions and is targeting a postseason return as a reliever.
American League Central
Chicago White Sox: The most improved team in baseball is desperately trying to hold off the Guardians and win a division title after finishing last two years in a row. Chicago has enjoyed good health and added journeyman outfielder Tommy Pham from the Phillies on Aug. 31. Pham was activated from the IL on Wednesday and could provide valuable postseason experience to complement his young new teammates — he has hit .315 in 37 career playoff games.
Hopeful return: Drew Thorpe was reinstated from the 60-day IL on Wednesday and is an intriguing option. The right-hander from Cal Poly SLO was a key piece in the 2024 trade that sent Dylan Cease to the Padres but has spent nearly two full seasons on the shelf. Now healthy, his inclusion on the playoff roster would be a gamble that his elite stuff can mask his inexperience.
Cleveland Guardians: Jo Adell didn’t come off the IL, but the addition of the former confounding Angels prospect in an August salary dump has bolstered the Guardians’ outfield — long a problem area. Adell has driven in 28 runs in 38 games with Cleveland and joins glittering rookie Chase DeLauter and steady veteran Steven Kwan in a productive outfield.
Hopeful return: Reliever Shawn Armstrong, who signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract last offseason, has been sidelined since July 24 with a calf strain. Barring a setback in his final minor league rehab appearance, he could be activated in time for the playoffs.
American League West
Houston Astros: Correa, whose second act with Houston has been a flop because of injuries, was working on an accelerated comeback from May ankle surgery. A few days ago team officials expressed optimism, but Tuesday they decided to shelve their shortstop when the ankle became inflamed after a workout. Houston is clinging to a one-game lead over the Texas Rangers in the AL West.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note.
Texas Rangers: Still in contention despite spending much of the season under .500, the Rangers welcomed back pitcher Nathan Eovaldi and third baseman Josh Jung from the injured list over the weekend. A calf strain had kept Jung sidelined since July 21 and Eovaldi had been out since Aug. 7 with elbow inflammation. Eovaldi, who has started in all but 20 of his 339 MLB appearances, will pitch out of the bullpen.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note
National League East
Atlanta Braves: Reynaldo López inflated hopes of a late-career surge when he posted a 1.99 ERA over 25 starts in his first season with Atlanta. But injuries — including right shoulder inflammation this season — have severely limited his contribution. López was placed on the IL again Tuesday.
Hopeful return: Bryce Elder had an arthroscopic procedure to clean up bone fragments in his right knee on Sept. 8. The hope is that the right-handed starter can recover quickly enough to be counted upon in the postseason.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.
Philadelphia Phillies: Although an MRI found no structural damage to the throwing shoulder of stalwart starter Jesús Luzardo, the left-hander remains a question for the playoffs. He was placed on the 15-day IL retroactive to Sept. 12, and it is doubtful he could pitch again in the regular season. Luzardo has a 2.87 ERA across 29 starts this season.
Hopeful return: Tanner Banks, a major contributor to the Philadelphia bullpen in 2025, was reinstated from the 60-day IL over the weekend. Although he wasn’t effective earlier this season, Banks is welcomed back because Phillies relievers have been poor against left-handed hitters.
National League Central
Milwaukee Brewers: Huntington Beach Marina High product Jake Bauers has suffered from shin splints almost all season, and the pain has kept him from playing the outfield lately. He can play first base, but that takes slugger Andrew Vaughn out of the lineup. Bauers, with 26 home runs and 83 RBIs, has been a key bat for Milwaukee. He has been particularly tough against the Dodgers, batting .348 with a .483 on-base percentage.
Hopeful return: Brandon Woodruff, one of the best starters in baseball when healthy, is rehabbing from shoulder inflammation that sidelined him in July. The Brewers are nearly guaranteed a first-round bye, giving Woodruff an extra week to build stamina.
Chicago Cubs: Shortstop and team leader Dansby Swanson will be welcomed back after missing a month with a left oblique injury. He is expected to rejoin the Cubs during their weekend series against the Cincinnati Reds.
Hopeful return: Left-handed starter Justin Steele is progressing through bullpen sessions and is almost ready to take the mound after missing the entire season with a left elbow flexor strain. Steele, whose record was 16-5 in 2023, likely would pitch from the bullpen in the postseason.
National League West
Dodgers: The loss of center fielder Andy Pages is significant. He can bat near the top or bottom of the order, displays power and speed, and had improved his patience at the plate enough to earn a career-high 45 walks in 128 games.
Hopeful return: Getting Ohtani healthy enough to produce at the plate is a priority, and his absence from the mound shouldn’t be felt if Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow pitch to their capabilities. Meanwhile, Edwin Diaz might not even make the playoff roster.
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
San Diego Padres: While recovering from Tommy John surgery, starter Joe Musgrove made it a goal to be ready for the postseason. Recovery difficulties between starts have made his status doubtful, however. Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, has pitched well in two starts since coming off the IL and appears ready.
Hopeful return: Ramón Laurenano, a 2025 trade deadline acquisition with a potent bat, last played May 30 because of hip inflammation. However, he told reporters that the chances of him playing in the postseason are “less than 5%.”
Arizona Diamondbacks: Zac Gallen was activated from the 60-day IL and Michael Soroka from the 15-day IL, giving the D-Backs two starters in their push to win a wild-card berth. Gallen, a proven starter who has been horrendous in 2026, has been out since the All-Star break with elbow inflammation. Soroka was out only two weeks with the same ailment.
Hopeful return: Third baseman Nolan Arenado suffered an injury to his left thumb Tuesday, the same injury he sustained in late August. It’s doubtful the injury would sideline the 14-year veteran with games this week being so important, yet the Diamondbacks have to hope the injury doesn’t impact his productivity.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.
Dodgers Starting Lineup
- Tommy Edman, CF
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Will Smith, C
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Teoscar Hernández, DH
- Miguel Rojas, 2B
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Kiké Hernández, 3B
- Alex Call, LF
Josue De Paula, Max Muncy and Alex Freeland are out of the lineup with the left-handed pitcher on the mound.
How to Watch Dodgers vs Reds on Wednesday
First pitch for Los Angeles Dodgers vs. Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, Sept. 16 is 3:40 p.m. PT/6:40 p.m. ET.
The game will be broadcast on SportsNet LA and in the MLB app.
The game will be broadcast on the radio on AM570 (in English) and KTNQ 1020 AM (in Spanish).

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers have glaring problems as playoffs approach — but also the threefold remedy
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series. Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen. There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers. Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball. No player influences the outcome of a game
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani sigue dando buenos pasos en su rehabilitación al realizar práctica de bateo desde este martes en Los Ángeles. El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, confirmó que la estrella nipona evoluciona favorablemente y se mantiene firme en su objetivo de volver a la acción antes del cierre de la temporada regular.
Sobre el doble agente del conjunto, expresó: «Shohei realizó sus swings en el tee y la respuesta física fue muy positiva (…) No tenemos una fecha exacta para su reaparición en el lineup, pero avanzamos con un progreso constante día a día. Lo importante es que el entrenamiento de hoy representó un avance claro», dijo.
El oriundo de Oshu, permanece en la lista de lesionados desde el pasado 8 de septiembre debido a una molestia muscular en el bíceps derecho y fue descartado para volver a lanzar durante la temporada debido a una lesión en su rodilla. La sesión de este martes marcó su primer trabajo con el bate desde que fue apartado de la plantilla activa.
Lee también: Yoshinobu Yamamoto sacó su poder en la lomita
Aunque el nipón no acompañó al conjunto angelino en su gira como visitante por Cincinnati, continúa completando su plan de trabajo y terapia médica en las instalaciones del conjunto de California.
Con el boleto a los playoffs ya asegurado para Los Ángeles, el cuerpo técnico confía en contar con Ohtani para los compromisos finales del calendario regular y ponerlo a punto de cara a la lucha por el título.

And it doesn’t get much easier with Blake Snell taking the mound, as the Dodgers are one win away from sweeping the Reds in a fourth straight series dating back to last year—counting both the regular season and playoffs. item.content:encoded:
The colloquially called “Great American Small Park” has looked awfully big for the Cincinnati Reds hitters facing the best pitching that the Dodgers have to offer. And it doesn’t get much easier with Blake Snell taking the mound, as the Dodgers are one win away from sweeping the Reds in a fourth straight series dating back to last year—counting both the regular season and playoffs.
Considering Sunday’s loss to the Marlins in which Emmet Sheehan pitched quite well, Dodger starters have held opponents scoreless through 20 innings, 14 of which have come against starters Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. On top of being dominant, Skubal and Yamamoto share the fact that they deviated somewhat from their regular approach in their last outing against the Reds, but in opposite directions—Skubal leaning more heavily on the fastball, while Yamamoto threw it even less than he normally does.
A critical distinction must be made between these two previous starters and Snell. Unlike the pair, Snell will be facing the Reds for the first time this season since he was not on the schedule in the three-game series at Dodger Stadium last week. And speaking of a track record against the Reds, Snell will have fond memories of his last time pitching at this stadium. Back in 2024, still with the Giants, Snell delivered one of the greatest outings of his career when he shut out the Reds in a 3-0 win—the two-time Cy Young winner punched out 11 in what, to this day, remains the only complete game and the only shutout of Snell’s illustrious career.
Wednesday game info
- Teams: Dodgers at Reds
- Ballpark: Great American Ball Park, Cincinnati
- Start time: 3:40 p.m. PT
- TV: SportsNet LA
- Radio: AM 570 (English), KTNQ 1020 AM (Spanish)

item.dc:creator: Sairuby Alayon Flores

El serpentinero toleró solo un imparable a lo largo de siete episodios para guiar la victoria de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles este martes por la noche, dejando a la escuadrade California a un paso de coronarse en la División Oeste del circuito viejo. Con este triunfo, el conjunto californiano colocó en dos su número mágico para adjudicarse su
item.content:encoded:
Este martes Yoshinobu Yamamoto sumó otro triunfo en la temporada, tras dominar a los Rojos de Cincinnati en el segundo duelo de la serie con blanqueada 4-0. El serpentinero toleró solo un imparable a lo largo de siete episodios para guiar la victoria de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles este martes por la noche, dejando a la escuadrade California a un paso de coronarse en la División Oeste del circuito viejo.
Con este triunfo, el conjunto californiano colocó en dos su número mágico para adjudicarse su decimotercer banderín divisional en los últimos catorce años. Tras sellar su clasificación a la postemporada el pasado lunes, Los Ángeles continúa en la pelea por la cima de la Liga Nacional.
Lee también: Astros pierden a Carlos Correa por lesión
Yamamoto quien cuenta con récord de 14-8 completó salida número 27 de la campaña (líder dentro del cuerpo de pitcheo del equipo) con efectividad de 2.67 en la temporada regular de 2026.
Posterior a ese batazo, el diestro retiró en fila a diez adversarios, concedió un par de pasaportes y recetó siete ponches. Es la segunda jornada consecutiva en la que un abridor de la tropa de California firma una labor de siete entradas en blanco, emulando lo hecho por Tarik Skubal el día anterior.
El cuerpo de serpentineros de los Dodgers firmó su blanqueada número 12 de la zafra, mientras que la ofensiva de los Rojos se quedó sin anotar por decimoséptima ocasión en el torneo.
Calma para los ajustes
Tras el encuentro el serpentinero japonés aseguró a la prensa: «Bueno, al principio no tenía muy buen control de mis sensaciones o mi mecánica, por lo que estuve un poco fuera de zona con la pelota. Pero mantuve la calma y la compostura, y fui capaz de hacer los ajustes a tiempo», expresó.
Tarik Skubal en el duelo anterior sentenció la victoria también por blanqueo en el primer duelo de la serie, sobre esto Yamamoto destacó que esa actuación lo animó a ser más firme en los pitcheos.
«Lo que hizo (Tarik Skubal) el lunes me dio una imagen muy positiva antes del encuentro de este martes. Me animó a ser agresivo y a atacar a los bateadores», dijo.

item.content:encoded:
Yamamoto (14-8) picked up the win in Tuesday's 4-0 victory over the Reds, allowing one hit and two walks over seven scoreless innings. He struck out seven.
The right-hander uncharacteristically walked the first two batters he faced, but Yamamoto would only let one other batter reach base before exiting after 91 pitches (55 strikes). The quality start was his 21st of the season, tied for the major-league lead with the Marlins' Sandy Alcantara, and over 10 starts since the All-Star break, Yamamoto has reeled off a 1.98 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 72:16 K:BB in 68.1 innings. He'll look to keep rolling in what will likely be his final outing of the regular season, at home early next week against the Padres.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yoshinobu Yamamoto Shows Dodgers Exactly Why He Should Start Game 1
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: When he needed it most, starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto reminded everyone in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse why he is the man for Game 1 of any playoff series. A day after the Dodgers clinched their postseason berth and secured a shot at completing their three-peat, Yamamoto took the mound to help the team in their postseason seeding race with a road game against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, September 16th. item.content:encoded:
When he needed it most, starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto reminded everyone in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse why he is the man for Game 1 of any playoff series.
A day after the Dodgers clinched their postseason berth and secured a shot at completing their three-peat, Yamamoto took the mound to help the team in their postseason seeding race with a road game against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, September 16th.
Yamamoto went seven scoreless innings, allowing one hit and two walks while getting eight punchouts, and looked like he had much more in the tank.
Manager Dave Roberts could have easily kept Yamamoto in for at least another inning; the Japanese pitcher had only 91 pitches down, given his propensity to pitch a high volume.
He allowed only two hard hits, highlighting his dominance, and both walks came on his first two batters.
Yamamoto retired 21 of the final 22 batters he faced, threw 16 whiffs, and used a wide variety of pitches, with none exceeding 25% usage.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto had another great outing, his best one in a while:
7 IP
1 H
2 BB
7 Ks
He looked great and could have gone another inning on just 91 pitches.
Quick and efficient from the Dodgers' ace. pic.twitter.com/pro7lpwsiK
The outing was a nice change of pace for Yamamoto, who has been prone to the long ball and giving up hard contact.
Instead, he did a good job of keeping the Reds hitters off-balance, and it looked like what Dodger fans have come to expect from Yamamoto: efficiency, elite pitch mix, and weak contact.
Why Dave Roberts Trusts Yamamoto
More than anything, his ability to move on from mistakes, like his lack of command that led to two walks right off the bat, is really the special sauce for Yamamoto.
Roberts, after the game, spoke to this resilience and how it translates perfectly to October and high-leverage moments, when everyone gets tested in some shape or fashion.
"I think the thing that I've learned about Yoshinobu is he's able to reset on the fly," the skipper said.
"He's able to bear down and make pitches when he needs to, to get a double play, a strikeout, a pop-up.
"Those are separators. When you're not totally locked in or in sync, you can still take a deep breath, reset, and navigate an inning and keep going. And so that's something that I've really learned from him."
Why Yamamoto Needed This Outing Now
Given his 2025 postseason exploits, it is hard to argue that Yamamoto has much to prove in the playoffs, and he needs to make his case to pitch the first game in the postseason.
Pitching in Game 1, when the team is fully healthy, is the ultimate nod of respect for an ace, and earning that honor as a member of his special rotation makes it all the more noteworthy.
Yamamoto, given his track record, has seemingly been in pole position all season, but Blake Snell's form and Tarik Skubal's arrival have sparked a healthy debate about who takes the ball first.
Since returning from the IL after elbow surgery on August 11th, Snell has a 1.04 ERA through 34.2 innings. He has 46 strikeouts and 14 walks in that span.
Yamamoto has a 1.98 ERA in 68.1 innings since the All-Star break. His ratio is 72 strikeouts to 16 walks.
By comparison, Skubal has a 2.52 ERA in 50 innings with the Dodgers since joining from the trade deadline on August 3rd. He also has a 57 strikeouts-to-11 walks ratio.
Recently, Skubal had his own seven-inning scoreless outing, and he looked very settled in, while Snell has not put a foot wrong.
However, Yamamoto's latest outing showed the front office that he can deliver a vintage Yamamoto outing, which, come postseason time, is invaluable.
It means he can provide a long outing, sometimes a complete game, along with minimal runs allowed, and leave the hitters in a tizzy.

After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set.
After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Yamamoto has amazed in his two most recent starts— both against the Reds— allowing just one run over 14 innings while racking up 17 strikeouts compared to just three walks.
Yamamoto held the Reds to just a 1-21 clip after walking his first two hitters of the game on Tuesday, and the right-hander managed to take a page out of Skubal’s playbook for his dominating efforts, notes Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
Yamamoto was able to learn from how the Reds approached Skubal the night before, and Snell was no doubt gathering similar information on Tuesday.
“That kind of encouraged me to be aggressive and attack the hitters,” Yamamoto said through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda.
The pitching has managed to hold their end of the bargain against Cincinnati this week, and Blake Snell looks to keep that trajectory in motion. On the offensive side of the ball, Teoscar Hernández has fortified the offense at Great American Ball Park, as the right-hander has crushed a pair of two-run home runs that put both games out of reach.
Hernández has once again found his stride that fans saw during spring training this year, and the Dodger outfielder’s recent success is the brainchild of hitting coach Aaron Bates, allowing Hernández to have a “twister tap” in his stride to the ball, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
Update on Shohei Ohtani
It’s an unusual feeling watching the Dodgers without Shohei Ohtani in the everyday lineup. So far, rookie Josue De Paula has filled in at DH to a small degree of success in limited time (.143/.368/.429, 19 PA) while the reigning two-time NL MVP recovers from multiple nagging issues.
Jack Harris of the California Post notes that Ohtani was able to take batting practice on Monday, and the team is optimistic that he can potentially return from the injured list before the end of the regular season.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”

item.title: [spectrumnews1.com] Dodgers beat Reds 4-0
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: CINCINNATI — Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed one hit through seven innings as the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-0 on Tuesday night to edge closer to an NL West division title. The Dodgers reduced the magic number to clinch their 13th division title in the past 14 seasons to two. Los Angeles wrapped up a playoff spot on Monday and still is vying for the top seed in the NL. item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed one hit through seven innings as the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-0 on Tuesday night to edge closer to an NL West division title.
The Dodgers reduced the magic number to clinch their 13th division title in the past 14 seasons to two. Los Angeles wrapped up a playoff spot on Monday and still is vying for the top seed in the NL.
Cincinnati is assured of a non-winning season after its 81st loss.
Yamamoto (14-8) made his team-high 27th start and allowed only a third-inning double to Elly De La Cruz, after which he retired 10 straight. He walked two and struck out seven. It was the second straight game a Dodgers starter went seven scoreless after Tarik Skubal on Monday.
Dodgers pitching recorded its 12th shutout of the season. The Reds were blanked for the 17th time.
Freddie Freeman returned to the Dodgers lineup after missing three of the past five games with right knee soreness and had three singles in five at-bats. Freeman was 3 for 30 coming into Tuesday.
Josue De Paula batted leadoff for the first time in just his fifth career game for the Dodgers and went 0 for 5 with a strikeout. He's 2 for 14 since his callup.
Teoscar Hernandez's 15th homer of the season off right-hander Rhett Lowder followed a walk to Kyle Tucker and made the score 3-0 in the third. Lowder (6-11) allowed three earned runs on five hits in five innings.
Alex Freeland made the score 4-0 in the seventh with a solo homer off Pierce Johnson.
De La Cruz extended his on-base streak to 22 games dating to Aug. 22, going 2 for 3 with a double, walk, and stolen base.
Cincinnati had runners on first and third in the ninth against Tanner Scott who struck out the next three batters to seal the Dodgers' ninth straight win over the Reds.
Dodgers LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91) will oppose Reds LHP Andrew Abbott (6-11, 4.84) on Wednesday.

item.content:encoded:
How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

Dodgers news: Freddie Freeman reveals all he's 'trying to do' before MLB playoffs appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Freddie Freeman returned to the Los Angeles Dodgers lineup on Tuesday for the second game of their series against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati.
The former National League Most Valuable Player missed three of the previous five Los Angeles games because of ongoing right knee soreness, but he managed to make an impact on the Dodgers' 4-0 victory over the Reds.
Freeman looked great with the bat in his return. He didn't score a run or drive one in, but he went 3-for-5. For now, the 37-year-old first baseman is looking to build momentum and reach his top form once the postseason rolls around.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"It was good. I've been kind of working, did a new thing in the cage the last couple of days, so gotta go for results-based things right now. We gotta get hot with two weeks to go, and looking to be hot for a few weeks. That's all I'm trying to do," the 10-time All-Star said in a postgame interview (via SportsNet LA)
Freeman is an undeniably integral part of the Dodgers' success in recent years, and he's expected to play a major role in the postseason, as Los Angeles takes aim at winning a World Series for the third year in a row.
That said, he's hitting just .100/.270/.200 with just a home run and three RBIs in nine games played so far in September. There is still a lot of time for him to get back to his usual form, with the Dodgers already assured of a spot in the playoffs.
Related: Dodgers' Dave Roberts gives props to Yoshinobu Yamamoto for savvy game vs. Reds
Related: Bobby Miller gets brutally honest on returning to Dodgers

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 4-pitch leadoff walk was a red flag, but the Dodgers' ace proved it was a fluke
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: CINCINNATI — Before each start, Yoshinobu Yamamoto does something remarkable. Many pitchers long toss as part of their pregame routine. item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Before each start, Yoshinobu Yamamoto does something remarkable.
Many pitchers long toss as part of their pregame routine. It's common practice at the high school level and above to warm up the arm, boot up the body, rev up the engine. Throwing a ball far is mighty similar, biomechanically, to throwing a ball fast.
But Yamamoto takes things to another level. After subjecting his muscles and ligaments to an elaborate stretching program, the Dodgers righty begins playing catch, gradually working his way toward the outer reaches of a big-league park's center-field grasslands. First 200 feet, then 250, 275, up to around 300. But instead of winding himself up with a few hop-steps like most long-tossers do, Yamamoto lets it fly from the relative standstill of his usual in-game windup.
It's a mesmerizing thing to witness — this 5-foot-10, 176-pound speck of cerulean catapulting a baseball 100 yards without the help of any real momentum. For a few seconds after release, Yamamoto stands frozen, balancing on his left leg with his right leg dangling in the air. The whole thing looks fake, like a lazy AI generation. How could a dude that small throw a ball that far that easily?
Such is the magic of Yamamoto: balance, intention, mechanical precision.
All those qualities and more were on display Tuesday in Cincinnati as the undersized hurler tore the Reds asunder. He worked seven scoreless innings, struck out seven and allowed just one hit.
After walking the first two hitters of the game, Yamamoto settled in. Following Elly De La Cruz's double in the third, the Dodgers starter retired the final 13 hitters he faced.
"He's able to reset on the fly. He's able to bear down and make pitches when he needs to," manager Dave Roberts explained after L.A.'s 4-0 win.
Yamamoto needed that adjustability Tuesday after an uncharacteristically poor start to the outing. He walked Cincinnati leadoff man Carlos Jorge, making just the fifth start of his MLB career, on four wayward offerings. It was the first time in Yamamoto's stateside tenure that he walked the first batter of the game on four pitches. He was similarly over-careful with the following hitter, walking De La Cruz on a 3-1 count. Jorge reached third base on a sac fly but got no further, as Yamamoto escaped the frame with no damage.
"At the beginning, because I [didn't] have my usual stuff mechanically, so mentally I was very calm, and then still kept composed, so I was able to make an adjustment on time," Yamamoto said afterward.
From there, it was business as usual, with Yamamoto deploying his typical barrage of splitters, curves and heaters. It was metronomical, almost humdrum, the way Yamamoto eased through the outing with little trouble. You blinked, and he was in the seventh with a zero on the board.
His entire season has carried a similar energy. The National League's overabundance of headline hurlers has been one of this campaign's main storylines. Jacob Misiorowski looks primed to win his first Cy Young behind a historic, bat-missing stat line. Chris Sale, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Chase Burns have all been excellent as well. Those characters, to a certain extent, have overshadowed Yamamoto's contributions.
This tumultuous Dodgers season, too, has stolen some of the shine. So much attention has been paid to the health and exploits of Shohei Ohtani and his quest to reestablish himself as a two-way dynamo over a full season. L.A.'s acquisition of Tarik Skubal overtook the trade deadline. Through it all, Yamamoto has remained magnificently consistent.
And with October just around the corner, the 2025 World Series hero is looking primed to carry the torch for the Dodgers once again.

item.title: [Diario Libre] VIDEO | Teoscar Hernández y Yoshinobu Yamamoto brillan, Dodgers a 2 triunfos de ganar la división
item.dc:creator: Diario Libre
item.description: Teoscar Hernández volvió a demostrar que atraviesa un momento ofensivo importante y encabezó la ofensiva de los Dodgers en la victoria 4-0 sobre los Reds este martes en el Great American Ball Park. item.content:encoded:
Teoscar Hernández volvió a demostrar que atraviesa un momento ofensivo importante y encabezó la ofensiva de los Dodgers en la victoria 4-0 sobre los Reds este martes en el Great American Ball Park.
El dominicano conectó un cuadrangular de dos carreras en la tercera entrada, su segundo vuelacercas en igual cantidad de partidos, para ampliar una ventaja que Los Ángeles ya no perdería.
Hernández terminó de 3-1 y produjo dos carreras, mientras los Dodgers se acercaron a solo dos victorias de asegurar el título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional.
El jonrón tuvo además un significado particular para Hernández, quien había tenido dificultades frente a los lanzadores derechos durante buena parte de la temporada. Hasta finales de agosto, registraba apenas .668 de OPS contra derechos, situación que incluso llevó al manager Dave Roberts a considerar un posible pelotón en el jardín izquierdo con jugadores recién ascendidos.
Después de conectar un jonrón ante el zurdo Framber Valdez en Detroit, Hernández trabajó con los coaches de bateo antes de la serie contra los Cardinals, y desde entonces su producción ha comenzado a cambiar.
Yamamoto intransitable
La actuación del dominicano sirvió como complemento perfecto para otra extraordinaria presentación de Yoshinobu Yamamoto. El japonés tuvo un comienzo poco habitual, al fallar ocho de sus primeros nueve lanzamientos y conceder boletos consecutivos a los dos primeros bateadores de Cincinnati. Fue apenas la cuarta ocasión esta temporada en que otorgó múltiples boletos en una entrada y la primera vez en su carrera de Grandes Ligas que abrió una salida con dos bases por bolas consecutivas.
Pero aquel descontrol inicial quedó rápidamente en el pasado. Después de poner a dos corredores en las bases en el primer episodio, Yamamoto solo permitió que otro bateador de Cincinnati llegara a salvo durante el resto de su actuación. Retiró a 21 de los últimos 22 bateadores que enfrentó y completó siete entradas en blanco, con apenas un hit permitido, un doble de Elly De La Cruz en el tercer inning, además de siete ponches.
La ofensiva angelina había tomado ventaja desde el segundo episodio, cuando Hunter Feduccia produjo una carrera con un sencillo. En el tercero llegó el batazo de Hernández para colocar el marcador 3-0 y, posteriormente, Alex Freeland agregó otro cuadrangular solitario para completar las cuatro carreras de Los Ángeles. El ataque de los Dodgers no fue especialmente abundante, pero produjo lo suficiente para respaldar a Yamamoto y convertir su actuación en una nueva joya monticular.
Para Yamamoto, fue además su tercera apertura consecutiva completando siete entradas y la quinta salida seguida en la que alcanzó al menos el séptimo episodio. Desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas, el derecho japonés ha mantenido un ritmo dominante, con efectividad de 1.98 en 68? entradas, 72 ponches y solo 16 boletos en 10 aperturas, una producción que lo coloca como una de las principales piezas de la rotación de Los Ángeles de cara a octubre.
La victoria dejó a los Dodgers con el número mágico en dos para conquistar su decimotercer título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional en las últimas 14 temporadas.
- Después de haber asegurado ya su boleto a la postemporada, Los Ángeles continúa ahora en busca de la corona divisional y de una posición privilegiada para octubre.
Blake Snell será el encargado de subir al montículo en el próximo encuentro de la serie, mientras los Dodgers siguen construyendo una rotación que, con Yamamoto al frente, vuelve a tomar protagonismo en su búsqueda de un tercer campeonato consecutivo.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers’ bullpen combine on 3-hit shutout to beat Reds

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — The Dodgers can only hope it looks this good in October.
One night after Tarik Skubal went seven innings in his first scoreless outing as a Dodger, Yoshinobu Yamamoto matched him, allowing only one hit in his seven scoreless innings as the Dodgers shut out the Cincinnati Reds, 4-0, on Tuesday night.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going tomorrow – you feel good about preventing runs,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
The win moved the Dodgers (92-59) within one day of clinching their 13th NL West division title in the past 14 seasons. Their magic number is one after the second-place San Diego Padres (82-69) lost to the Colorado Rockies later Tuesday night.
The Dodgers’ lead over the Atlanta Braves (89-63) for the No. 2 seed in the National League remains 3½ games. Their magic number to clinch a first-round bye is eight.
All of that makes the final two weeks of the regular season a chance for the Dodgers to get things right for October and their three-peat pursuit. The starting rotation appears to be there already.
Skubal has a 1.73 ERA over his past four starts. With Tuesday’s outing, Yamamoto’s ERA is 1.79 over his past seven starts. Blake Snell starts on Wednesday – and he has given up a total of only four runs in six starts since returning from elbow surgery. Only fourth starter Tyler Glasnow (eight runs in 10 innings over his past two starts) seems to have some work to do before being October-ready.
“Yeah, pretty good,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said after his first three-hit game since Aug. 17. “You have Blake Snell going tomorrow. Tyler on the back end of that too. Roki’s on his way back.
“It’s a special pitching staff. It really is. So as an offense, we just need to score a few runs for them, just like we did last year.”
Yamamoto started Tuesday by giving the Reds hope – he walked the first two batters he faced – then he took it away, retiring 21 of the next 22 batters he faced.
“They took a little moment for me,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter of the mound visit from catcher Hunter Feduccia and pitching coach Mark Prior that followed the walks. “They came up to me and, ‘Hey, how you doing?’ and just checked in on me. And then I was able to get back to my normal rhythm.”
Elly De La Cruz had the only hit off Yamamoto, a double into the left-field corner with two outs in the third inning.
But even that was a victory – Yamamoto kept him in the ballpark after De La Cruz had hit a home run in each of the previous four games between the Dodgers and Reds. He then retired the next 13 batters in order, getting six of his seven strikeouts.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine. Not giving these guys too much credit. And yeah, at first, it didn’t look promising as far as pitch count, the two walks. But then he kind of dialed things in, like he’s been known to do.”
The Dodgers gave him a lead in the second inning when Max Muncy was hit by a pitch and Tommy Edman and Hunter Feduccia followed with singles. They added to it in the third inning with a two-run home run from Teoscar Hernandez, who remains hot – 24 for 63 (.381) in his past 18 games.
“It’s been very helpful,” Roberts said of Hernandez’s late-season renaissance. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. The last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him. The defense ticked up. The at-bat quality, the taking walks, all of it. I can’t say enough about what he’s done the last 10 days.”
De La Cruz had another hit, a single in the ninth inning that put runners on the corners for the Reds with no outs. Tanner Scott struck out Sal Stewart, Jose Trevino and Eugenio Suarez to close out the shutout.

item.title: [New York Post] Yoshinobu Yamamoto rounds into playoff form as Dodgers move to cusp of NL West title
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: CINCINNATI –– There’s not much the Dodgers can do, manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday afternoon, to get their all-important rotation ready for the added workload that will come in the postseason. Over the final couple weeks of the regular season, they have to just keep running their starters out there, and counting on them to round into elevated October form. That’s what appeared to happen with Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Tuesday night at Great American Ball Park, in what was the right-hander’s most do
item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– There’s not much the Dodgers can do, manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday afternoon, to get their all-important rotation ready for the added workload that will come in the postseason.
Over the final couple weeks of the regular season, they have to just keep running their starters out there, and counting on them to round into elevated October form.
That’s what appeared to happen with Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Tuesday night at Great American Ball Park, in what was the right-hander’s most dominant performance of at least the last couple months.
In the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, Yamamoto threw a one-hit masterpiece over seven scoreless innings, flashing the kind of ruthless efficiency that defined his heroics during last year’s playoffs.
After walking his first two batters in the first inning, he retired 21 of the 22 after with seven strikeouts and virtually no stress.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine.”
The reigning World Series MVP hadn’t exactly been struggling lately, of course. Just last week, he held the Reds to one run over seven innings with 10 strikeouts back in Los Angeles.
But what Yamamoto did on Tuesday was different, keyed by quick and easy outs on soft and harmless contact.
It’s what he did as the ace of last year’s postseason staff, and what he will need to do again as the Dodgers go for a World Series three-peat this fall.
“I’d like to carry this,” Yamamoto said through an interpreter of his renewed stuff, “into October.”
The Dodgers are hoping they won’t have to ask as much out of Yamamoto this time around; that they need him to pitch back-to-back complete games (like he did in Game 2 of the NLCS and Game 2 of the World Series) or provide back-to-back nights of season-saving heroics (following up a victorious Game 6 start in the Fall Classic with a winning three-inning appearance out of the bullpen in Game 7).
But in a postseason environment, it’s impossible to know what exactly will be required.
“You can’t just try to create that during the regular season because you want these guys as strong and healthy for the October run [as possible],” Roberts said pregame. “But it’s one of those things that, once we get to the postseason, all bets are off and everyone is going to do what they can to contribute.”
It would help, of course, if the Dodgers’ currently Shohei Ohtani-less offense can keep turning a corner, with Tuesday bringing more positive –– albeit subtle –– signs.
The biggest development: Freddie Freeman returned to the lineup amid his ongoing right knee injury, and finally snapped out of a 3-for-30 slump by collecting three singles in the first, fifth and seventh innings.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday,” Roberts said, after Freeman missed his third game in the last week on Monday, “which is a good thing.”
The Dodgers’ scoring, meanwhile, came from elsewhere.

Hunter Feduccia laced an RBI single in the second off Reds starter Rhett Lowder, maintaining his unexpected status as the Dodgers’ best hitter against right-handed pitching since being re-acquired at the trade deadline (with a team-leading .292 average in such splits since the start of August).
Teoscar Hernández continued his late-season surge with a two-run homer in the third, giving him four home runs, eight extra-base hits, 18 RBIs and a .417 average over his last 14 games.
Even Alex Freeland chipped in with a solo blast in the seventh and a double in the ninth, helping him outshine fellow rookie Josue De Paula (who went 0-for-5 with his first two strikeouts of the season after getting bumped up to the leadoff spot).
That was all enough to help the team lower its magic number to clinch the National League West to one.
Still, when it comes to October, no position group will be more important than the Dodgers’ rotation.
That’s why, right now, outings like the one Yamamoto made on Tuesday, or Tarik Skubal spun the night before (also seven scoreless innings) are the most promising ways the Dodgers can ramp up toward the playoffs.
Once they get there, they’ll need their starters to be on.

item.content:encoded:
【ドジャース4-0レッズ】シンシナティ／グレートアメリカンボールパーク、9月15日（日本時間16日）
前日の勝利で14年連続のポストシーズン進出を決めたドジャースは敵地でのレッズ4連戦の2戦目。地区優勝が目前に迫る中、山本由伸が今季27度目の先発マウンドに上がった。前回登板でもレッズを相手に7回3安打1失点、10三振の好投を披露した右腕が、この日も相手打線を寄せつけない投球を見せ、4-0で勝利。山本は7回91球を投げて1安打無失点、7三振の内容で自己最多をさらに更新する14勝目（8敗、防御率2.51）を挙げた。 山本は初回、先頭から2者連続四球で得点圏に走者を背負ったものの、後続を抑えて無失点でスタート。すると打線は二回、1死からマックス・マンシーの死球とトミー・エドマンのヒットでチャンスを作り、ハンター・フェデューシアがセンターへのタイムリーを放って1点を先制した。 三回は1死からカイル・タッカーが四球で出塁し、続くテオスカー・ヘルナンデスがレフトスタンドへ2試合連発となる15号2ラン。リードを3点に広げ、山本を援護した。 援護を受けた山本は、三回2死からエリー・デラクルーズに初安打となる二塁打を許したが、新人王候補のサル・スチュワートを空振り三振に仕留めて無失点。その後はレッズ打線につけ入る隙を与えず、スコアボードにゼロを並べ続けた。 ドジャースは七回1死からアレックス・フリーランドの4号ソロで1点を追加。山本は七回も三者凡退に抑え、7回1安打無失点と前回登板に続いてレッズ打線を圧倒した。 ドジャースは八回を2番手のブロック・スチュワートが無失点に抑えると、最終回は3番手のタナー・スコットがマウンドへ。ところが、先頭の代打デーン・マイヤーズに四球を与えると、続くデラクルーズにはセンター前に運ばれ、無死一、三塁のピンチとなった。しかし、後続を3者連続三振に抑えて4-0で試合終了。この試合が終了した時点で地区優勝へのマジックナンバーを「2」とした。

item.content:encoded:
Elly De La Cruz is truly ascending into Tungsten Arm O'Doyle territory of late.
Monday night saw him completely destroy a baseball, one that was conservatively estimated at 457 feet as it buzzed past the power stacks in left-center field in Great American Ball Park en route to exiting the stadium altogether. It was reminiscent of the superblast he hit from the other side of the plate off Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal just a week ago, feats of strength irreplicable by just about any other sole on the planet.
The Cincinnati Reds lost last night, though. Elly's homer was their lone run in a 4-1 loss to those very same Dodgers, a loss that officially eliminated the Reds from any miracle chance at a spot in the postseason. It also sunk them to 10 full games under .500 at 70-80, and this season is rapidly deteriorating into yet another one to forget and chuck onto the scrap-heap of memories of this once proud franchise.
I digress.
Rhett Lowder has a lot to improve upon as he heads into a vital offseason for his overall development. Anything short of a rapid change of form means the Reds need to build in even more redundancy in their starting depth plans for 2027, and there's been precious little in the way of advancement from their former 1st round pick so far in his own disappointing 2026. He'll get the start tonight, while the Dodgers will counter with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
First pitch in GABP is set for 6:40 PM ET. Here's how both teams will line up:

| Y. Yamamoto – RHP | Rhett Lowder – RHP |

item.title: [True Blue LA] Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the rock of the Dodgers rotation
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen

item.content:encoded:
Yoshinobu Yamamoto takes the mound on Tuesday night against the Reds in what figures to be his penultimate start of the regular season. It’s been another fantastic year, once again the anchor of the Dodgers rotation, the only member to stay healthy and make every start this season.
Yamamoto enters Tuesday with 172 innings, only five outs shy of his MLB career high set last year. With two starts left, this year figures to settle into his third-most innings in a season, counting his time pitching for Orix in Japan, with 193 2/3 innings in 2021 and 193 innings in 2022, winning the first two of his three consecutive Eiji Swamura Awards as the best pitcher in Japan.
Unless Justin Wrobleski finds a way to cram 28 2/3 innings into these final 12 games, Yamamoto will once again be the only Dodgers pitcher to qualify for leaderboards, with at least one inning per team game played. Prior to Yamamoto this year and last, no other Dodgers starting pitcher qualified since 2022, when both Julio Urías and Tyler Anderson did so.
Yamamoto this year has the 10th qualifying season by a Dodgers pitcher dating back to 2017, an average of one qualifier per year though going four seasons without (2018, 2020, 2023, 2024) over the last decade. But here’s a fun little quirk: eight of the previous nine Dodgers pitchers to have enough innings to qualify all got Cy Young Award votes in that season.
Dodgers qualifying pitchers 2017-26
| Pitcher | Year | Innings | CYA finish | CYA votes |
| Clayton Kershaw | 2017 | 175 | 2nd | 3 1st, 25 2nd, 1 3rd, 1 4th |
| Hyun-jin Ryu | 2019 | 182.7 | 2nd | 1 1st, 10 2nd, 8 3rd, 7 4th, 3 5th |
| Clayton Kershaw | 2019 | 178.3 | 8th | 1 3rd |
| Walker Buehler | 2019 | 182.3 | 9th | 1 4th |
| Walker Buehler | 2021 | 207.7 | 4th | 2 2nd, 9 3rd, 17 4th, 1 5th |
| Julio Urías | 2021 | 185.7 | t-6th | 3 5th |
| Julio Urías | 2022 | 175 | 3rd | 7 2nd, 9 3rd, 5 4th, 1 5th |
| Tyler Anderson | 2022 | 178.7 | n/a | n/a |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 2025 | 173.7 | 3rd | 16 3rd, 11 4th, 2 5th |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 2026 | 172+ | TBD | TBD |
If we extend this back to 2013, 14 of the last 19 Dodgers pitchers to qualify received Cy Young Award votes, thanks to Clayton Kershaw and Zack Greinke each faring well in each of their three seasons as teammates (2013-15).
This season, Jacob Milwaukee Brewers ace Misiorowski is a lock for the National League Cy Young Award, and there is stiff competition with Chris Sale, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo, and others all likely to receive votes as well. But there are five spots on each ballot, and 30 ballots for each league, so “receiving votes” shouldn’t be too high of a bar to clear for Yamamoto this year.
In the list above, Kershaw and Walker Buehler each received a lone vote in 2019, for third and fourth place, respectively, for instance.
Yamamoto entering Tuesday leads the majors in averaging 6.62 innings per start, with his 23 starts lasting at least six inning second-most in the majors, as are his 11 starts of at least seven innings. Yamamoto’s four starts of at least eight innings are tied for most in MLB.
Yamamoto is third in the National League in ERA (2.62) and xERA (3.05), sixth in innings (172), 10th in strikeouts (171), and ninth in strikeout-minus-walk rate (20.1 percent). Yamamoto is also tied for fourth in Baseball Reference WAR (5.4) with Sale, and is tied for fifth in the NL in FanGraphs WAR (4.3) with Reds right-hander Chase Burns.
Tuesday game info
- Teams: Dodgers at Reds
- Ballpark: Great American Ball Park, Cincinnati
- Start time: 3:40 p.m. PT
- TV: SportsNet LA
- Radio: AM 570 (English), KTNQ 1020 AM (Spanish)
